### 13.13 Secrets: one way to store and load API keys (decided with the owner 2026-11-11)

`bxrig secrets` is the single way to keep API keys and tokens. Every machine uses the same commands; `export`/`import` (later) moves them between machines.

|                    Command                    |                                                                Does                                                                |
|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `secrets status`                              | backend in use, whether a keyring is available, how many secrets are stored                                                        |
| `secrets set NAME [--from-file=F]`            | stores a value: typed hidden at the terminal, or read from a file. Never a command-line value. Replaces an existing one            |
| `secrets list`                                | names only, with the coding agent that reads each known key                                                                        |
| `secrets get NAME [--show]`                   | says whether it is set and its length; `--show` prints the value                                                                   |
| `secrets unset NAME --yes`                    | deletes a value (plan without `--yes`, exit 2)                                                                                     |
| `secrets run [NAMES...] [--strict] -- CMD...` | runs CMD with those secrets in its own environment only; exit code is CMD's. A name that is not set is skipped, `--strict` exits 4 |
| `secrets env [NAMES...]`                      | prints `export NAME='value'` lines for `eval` (all stored names when none given)                                                   |

* Names are environment variable names: capital letters, digits, underscores (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`).
* Backend: the desktop keyring through `secret-tool` (libsecret) when `secret-tool` exists and `org.freedesktop.secrets` is on the user D-Bus (running or activatable); otherwise private files (`~/.local/share/bxrig/secrets/NAME`, mode 600 in a mode 700 folder). The choice is saved in `~/.config/bxrig/secrets.json` and shown by `status`. Keyring entries carry the attributes `service=bxrig name=NAME`.
* Values are passed to `secret-tool` and to programs through standard input and the process environment, never through a command line, a temp file, a log, or `answers.json`.
* `set` is interactive on purpose and needs no `--yes`.
* Exit codes: 0 done, 2 usage or plan without `--yes`, 4 precondition (bad name, secret not set, no value), 6 the store failed. Loading into shells (default is per command, global is opt-in per key):
* `secrets apply [--yes]` writes `~/.config/bxrig/secrets.sh` (bash, zsh) and `secrets.fish`. They hold no values: one wrapper per agent command whose key is stored (`claude() { bxrig secrets run ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -- command claude "$@"; }`). `secrets set` runs it automatically. The shell init templates source these files.
* `secrets global on NAME --yes | off NAME | show`: exports a key to every new shell. `on` prints a warning first (every program, including AI agents and what they run, can read it). The values go to a session cache, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bxrig-secrets.env` and `.fish` (mode 600, tmpfs, wiped at logout), never to a config file. The loader files call `secrets unlock` once per login when the cache is missing (the keyring's single unlock prompt); `secrets lock` removes the cache. A globally exported key gets no wrapper. Moving machines and the keyring:
* `secrets export FILE [--plain] [--force] --yes`: all stored secrets as `export NAME='value'` lines, encrypted with a passphrase by `age -p` (age asks on the terminal; the file is mode 600). `--plain` writes a readable .env instead (mode 600; the plan says so). An existing file is kept unless `--force`.
* `secrets import FILE [--overwrite] --yes`: reads an age file or a .env file; the plan lists each name as new, same or differs. A name that already has a different value is kept unless `--overwrite`. New machine: `install.sh`, `init --answers answers.json`, `secrets import`, `dotfiles apply`.
* `secrets setup [--keyring=kwallet|gnome-keyring|none] [--yes] [--dry-run]`: checks for a Secret Service on the user D-Bus (running or activatable). Installs `libsecret` (`secret-tool`, repo core) and `age` (repo extra) when missing; when no keyring exists, also `kwallet` on Plasma or `gnome-keyring` elsewhere, or the one named. `--keyring=none` installs no keyring and saves the file backend. The plan names what it installs. Package names and `secret-tool` in libsecret were checked on archlinux.org on 2026-11-11. Secret types and providers (decided with the owner 2026-11-11):
* Every secret has a **type** : `ai` (a key for an AI provider) or `other` (a GitHub token and so on). A name in the provider registry is `ai` automatically; any other name is `other` unless `secrets set NAME --type=ai [--provider=ID]` says otherwise. The type and provider are kept in `secrets.json` (`meta`, names only, never values). `secrets list [--type=ai|other]` filters; `secrets run --type=ai -- CMD` loads every AI key and no other secret.
* The provider registry (`AiProviders`) maps providers to environment variables: anthropic `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, openai `OPENAI_API_KEY`, google `GEMINI_API_KEY`, openrouter `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, novita `NOVITA_API_KEY`, opencode `OPENCODE_API_KEY`, groq, mistral, deepseek, xai, together (`GROQ_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY`, `TOGETHER_API_KEY`). Names are from models.dev (the registry OpenCode uses), checked 2026-11-11.
* Each agent declares the providers it accepts (`AiAgents`): Claude Code anthropic, Codex openai, Gemini CLI google, OpenCode all of the above. **An agent is only ever given keys from its own list.** Its wrapper carries the stored ones among them (`opencode() { bxrig secrets run ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY -- command opencode "$@"; }`); nothing else is loaded.
* Tests: `tests/secrets-test.sh` (fake `secret-tool` and `busctl`). The registry of agent key names is from the vendors' documentation and the user can store any other valid name.

### 13.14 AI agents (decided with the owner 2026-11-11)

`bxrig ai` knows four coding agents (`AiAgents`): `claude-code` (command `claude`), `codex-cli` (`codex`), `gemini-cli` (`gemini`), `opencode-cli` (`opencode`), each with the providers whose keys it accepts (see 13.13). Command names were checked in the Arch packages (`openai-codex` ships `/usr/bin/codex`, `gemini-cli` ships `/usr/bin/gemini`; `claude-code` comes from the CachyOS repo). The key names are from the vendors' documentation.

|                                Command                                |                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Does                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ai list`                                                             | each agent: installed, key stored, default                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `ai default [ID] [--yes]`                                             | shows the default, or sets it (the agent must be installed; plan without `--yes`, exit 2). Saved in `~/.config/bxrig/ai.json`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `ai launch [ID] [--dry-run]`                                          | opens the agent (the default when no ID) in your default terminal as `TERMINAL [-e] bxrig secrets run KEY -- COMMAND`, detached. The terminal is the first line of `~/.config/xdg-terminals.list` if it names a terminal BxRig knows and it is installed, else the first installed one. ghostty, alacritty and konsole get `-e`; kitty and foot get the command directly (foot and konsole flags are from memory, not verified here) |
| `ai shell [toggle\|status] [--backend=hyprland\|yakuake] [--dry-run]` | the pull-down AI shell: one shortcut shows and hides a terminal running your default agent (your shell when none is set); it keeps its session while hidden                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Pull-down AI shell.** The backend follows the desktop: a Hyprland session (`HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE`) uses a special workspace, KDE Plasma uses Yakuake; `--backend` overrides. Exit 4 when neither applies, when no terminal can carry a window class, or when Yakuake is missing.

* **Hyprland:** the first call starts a terminal with the window class `com.bxrig.ai` (ghostty `--class=`, kitty and alacritty `--class`, foot `--app-id`; konsole cannot) running `bxrig secrets run KEYS -- AGENT`, then sizes it to 100% x 45% and moves it to the top with `hyprctl dispatch resizewindowpixel` / `movewindowpixel` (best effort). The Hyprland module (`keys apply`) holds `hl.window_rule({ name = "bxrig-ai", match = { class = "^com.bxrig.ai$" }, workspace = "special:ai", float = true })` and the shortcut ```Super+\`` running```bxrig ai shell`. Later calls toggle the workspace:`hyprctl dispatch togglespecialworkspace ai`, and if that fails the Lua form`hl.dsp.workspace.toggle_special("ai")`. Window class is the ghostty config option`class\` (GTK builds), and it must look like a GTK application id, hence the dotted name.
* **Plasma (Yakuake):** the first call starts Yakuake, waits for its D-Bus name, adds a tab (`org.kde.yakuake.addSession` on `/yakuake/sessions`), types the agent command (`runCommand`) and shows the window (`toggleWindowState` on `/yakuake/window`); later calls only toggle. The tab is remembered in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bxrig-ai-shell`. `init` installs `yakuake` (official `extra`) when Plasma and an agent are chosen. The Plasma shortcut is not written by BxRig: bind `bxrig ai shell` in System Settings, Shortcuts (Yakuake also has its own open/retract key).
* **Not verified on a real desktop:** the Hyprland window rule and dispatchers in Lua mode, the percentage resize and move, the special-workspace slide direction, and Yakuake's `runCommand` (its changelog mentions a security prompt). They are on the acceptance checklist.
* Tests: `tests/ai-shell-test.sh` (fake `hyprctl`, `dbus-send`, `yakuake` and terminals).

**Agent sessions (tmux).** `ai session start [ID] [--name=N] [--dir=PATH] [--dry-run]` starts a detached tmux session `bxrig-AGENT[-N]` running the agent (the default when no ID) in PATH (the current folder by default) through `secrets run`, so it keeps working after you close the terminal. A session that already exists is reported, not replaced. `ai session list` shows only `bxrig-` sessions. `ai session attach NAME` joins one (NAME is the full name or what follows `bxrig-`; needs a terminal; detach with the tmux prefix then `d`). `ai session stop NAME --yes` ends one (plan without `--yes`, exit 2). Names are letters, digits, `-`, `_` (up to 40). Exit 4: tmux or the agent missing, bad name, no such session; 6: a tmux command failed. `init` installs `tmux` when an agent is chosen. Tests: `tests/ai-session-test.sh`.

**Local models (Ollama).** `ai models list` and `ai models ps` run `ollama list` and `ollama ps`; `ai models pull NAME` downloads a model with Ollama's own progress (the service must be running); `ai models rm NAME --yes` deletes one; `ai models status` says whether Ollama is installed and its service active; `ai models enable [--yes] [--dry-run]` runs `sudo systemctl enable --now ollama` (the package ships `ollama.service`, checked in the Arch file list 2026-11-11). Model names are letters, digits and `. _ : / -` and are passed as one argument, never through a shell. Exit 4: Ollama missing or bad name; otherwise Ollama's exit code. Wizard: `ai_ollama_service` (confirm, default yes) and `ai_models` (text, comma separated, empty by default) appear when Ollama is ticked; `init` runs `ai models enable`, then one **optional** `ai models pull` per name, so a failed or skipped download never stops the plan. Model names are not checked against Ollama's library (they change), only for safe characters.

Exit codes: 0 done, 2 usage or plan without `--yes`, 4 precondition (unknown or missing agent, no default, no terminal), 6 failed. Tests: `tests/ai-test.sh`, `tests/init_plan_test.bxs`, `tests/init-test.sh`.

Local models: AUR names were checked on 2026-11-11 (`lmstudio-bin`, `jan-bin`, `koboldcpp`, `gpt4all-chat`); Ollama is in `extra`, with `ollama-cuda` and `ollama-rocm` as add-ons that depend on `ollama`. Open WebUI is left out: its AUR package is flagged out of date. Starting the Ollama service and pulling models is later work.

Init rules for this page: a default agent that was not ticked is installed too; `secrets setup` runs whenever an agent is chosen (it installs a keyring only if none exists); the key steps are **optional**, so one that cannot run (no terminal, you press Enter to skip) is reported as skipped with the command to run later and the plan goes on.

An edited unit is never overwritten (exit 4). `unmount` disables and stops it and deletes the unit only while it is still the text BxRig wrote. Exit 4: rclone or fuse3 missing, unknown remote. The wizard's `cloud_storage` (default no) installs `rclone` and `fuse3`. Package facts checked on archlinux.org 2026-11-12. Not run against a real remote here. Tests: `tests/runtime-cloud-test.sh`.

### 13.24 System-aware wizard and `status`

`bxrig status [--json]` (read-only, exit 0) shows what the machine already has in the wizard's terms: detected answers per question (desktops from installed packages, shell from `$SHELL`, default terminal from `xdg-terminals.list`, default browser from `xdg-settings`, AI default, runner, container engine, installed apps per question) and the default apps still missing (the Resolver with the shell and root filesystem). `--json` data: `detected` (id, label, page, value), `installed_catalog_apps`, `default_apps_missing`.

`bxrig init` on a set-up machine starts from your saved answers merged with that scan (`tune`, the default): lists are joined, single choices follow the system when it says something, installed options show `✓ installed`. `--rerun` uses the saved answers only, `--fresh` the defaults, `--from=FILE` replaces the saved answers with a file (answers exported on another machine). Nothing the machine has is ever removed. The plan output splits `apps` into to install and already installed. `init --from-system --print-answers [--json]` prints the scan merged over the saved answers.

### 13.30 One-line installer, update channels, updates and notifications (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **One line:** `curl -fsSL https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/bxrig/install.sh | bash` (`bootstrap/web-install.sh` is published as `install.sh`). It shows the BxRig wordmark in the cyan to green gradient, the tagline and "Powered by BoxLang", checks the machine (CachyOS or Arch, not root, x86_64, sudo), downloads the channel's `bxrig-linux-x86_64` and `bootstrap.tar.gz`, verifies the Ed25519 signature of the release information (`version-latest.properties.sig`, OpenSSL, public key embedded in the published script) and the SHA-256 of both files against it, runs the stages of `bootstrap/install.sh` (`packages`, `toolchains`, `binary --binary`, `core`) behind spinners, then the setup wizard. There is no custom menu: it installs everything the wizard's defaults call for. Log: `~/.cache/bxrig/install.log`.
* **No human input:** `... | bash -s -- --yes [--answers FILE] [--channel stable|beta] [--no-wizard]`. `--yes` never asks (it needs passwordless sudo or a primed `sudo -v`), the wizard then runs `bxrig init --answers FILE --yes` or, without a file, `bxrig init --defaults --yes` (the wizard's default answers). `--dry-run` shows the banner and checks and does nothing. `--base-url` or `BXRIG_BASE_URL` points elsewhere. Exit 1 on any failure (nothing is installed after a failed checksum), 2 when you decline.
* **Channels and S3 (`downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/bxrig/`):** `stable/` (a `v*` tag), `beta/` (every push to `development`, the bleeding edge), each with `bxrig-linux-x86_64`, `.sha256`, `bootstrap.tar.gz`, `.sha256` and `version-latest.properties` (`version`, `commit`, `sha256`, `channel`, `builtAt`); `snapshots/<version>-<sha>/` keeps every beta build and `releases/<version>/` every stable one (uploads never delete). CI job 6 publishes when the AWS secrets exist (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_ACCESS_SECRET`).
* **`update check [--notify]`:** compares the running binary's SHA-256 with the channel's `version-latest.properties`; exit 10 when an update is available, 0 when current, 5 when the server is unreachable; also counts pending system updates (`checkupdates`). `update apply [--yes]` downloads the channel's binary, verifies its SHA-256 against its `.sha256` and the signed release information, and replaces the installed binary atomically (exit 5 on a mismatch or a bad signature, the old binary stays). `update channel [stable|beta]` shows or sets the channel (`~/.config/bxrig/update.json`; the wizard asks `update_channel`, default stable). `update notifications on|off|status` manages a daily user timer `bxrig-update-check.timer` that runs `update check --notify` and shows a notification (`noctalia msg notification-show`, else `notify-send`); the wizard asks `update_notifications`, default on. `system update [--yes]` takes a snapshot first when snapper or timeshift is present, then `sudo pacman -Syu --noconfirm` and, with yay, `yay -Sua --noconfirm`. The menu has Settings entries for check, apply, both channels, notifications on and off, and system update.
* **Signing (owner decision 2026-11-13: sign the installer and update):** CI signs every `version-latest.properties` and `install.sh` with Ed25519 (`openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin`) using the secret `BXRIG_SIGNING_KEY`; the properties carry `sha256` (binary) and `bootstrap_sha256` (bundle). The public key is `keys/release.pub` (made with `scripts/gen-signing-key.sh`), embedded into the binary (`bootstrap/gen-releasekey.sh` writes `src/bxrig/ReleaseKey.bx`) and into the published `install.sh` (CI replaces `@@PUBKEY_B64@@`). With a key a missing or invalid signature, or a file that does not match the signed hash, stops the install or update before anything changes (exit 1 for the installer, 5 for `update`); without a key (a development build) only SHA-256 is checked. Limit: the very first `curl | bash` still trusts the script it downloads (TLS and the bucket), so the signature protects the files the script fetches and every later update; verify `install.sh.sig` by hand with `keys/release.pub` for a stricter first install.
* Tests: `tests/web-install-test.sh` (fake server and stages, signed and unsigned), `tests/update-test.sh`, `init_plan_test.bxs`.

Like `runner set` these are settings: they act at once (no `--yes`). Exit: 0 done, 2 bad usage or mode, 4 unknown or invalid theme (nothing is written), 6 a file could not be written.
* **Theme format:** an Omarchy theme folder, so themes move both ways: `colors.toml`, optional `neovim.lua`, optional `backgrounds/` (the first file is the wallpaper). Both `colors.toml` shapes are read: the named one of Omarchy 4 master (`accent background foreground selection muted red green yellow blue magenta cyan bright_*`, `mode = "dark"|"light"`) and the older `color0..color15` one. The named shape maps to the 16 ANSI slots as Omarchy's terminal templates do. A missing required key or a value that is not `#rrggbb` rejects the whole theme. Light or dark is the file's `mode`, else the background luminance (above 0.4 is light).
* **Sources, first match wins:** `~/.config/bxrig/themes/NAME` (installed or imported), `~/.config/omarchy/themes/NAME` and `~/.local/share/omarchy/themes/NAME` (found on disk), then 15 bundled in the binary: 10 from Omarchy (catppuccin, catppuccin-latte, tokyo-night, gruvbox, nord, rose-pine, kanagawa, everforest, matte-black, flexoki-light; MIT, credited in `themes/NOTICE.md`) and 5 of ours (`bxrig`, `bxrig-light`, `bxrig-midnight`, `bxrig-cyan`, `bxrig-forest`). `install` takes an https git URL only (a repository named `omarchy-NAME-theme` becomes `NAME`), clones it shallow, validates it, refuses symlinks and an existing theme (without `--force`), and copies it without `.git`. Only your own themes can be removed, never the current one.
* **What `set` writes** (through the config service: atomic, backed up, journalled; unchanged files are skipped): the Noctalia palette `~/.config/noctalia/palettes/BxRigTheme.json` (the 16 roles are derived from the theme, both variants carry the same colours), `~/.config/bxrig/theme/{ghostty,kitty.conf,alacritty.toml,foot.ini,hypr.lua}`, `~/.config/btop/themes/bxrig.theme`, `~/.local/state/bxrig/current/theme/neovim.lua` and every theme's `neovim.lua` in `~/.config/bxrig/nvim-themes/`. Then it tells the desktop: `noctalia msg color-scheme-set custom BxRigTheme`, `theme-mode-set`, `wallpaper-set` (a bundled BxRig theme brings one of our wallpapers, an on-disk theme its `backgrounds/`, other bundled themes keep yours), `plasma-apply-colorscheme BreezeDark|BreezeLight` on KDE, `hyprctl reload` inside Hyprland. A missing or silent Noctalia is a note, not an error. Mode `theme` (default) follows the theme; `dark`, `light` or `auto` pin it; the mode survives `set`.
* **Where the files are used:** the terminal starters (written once) include `~/.config/bxrig/theme/...` (ghostty `config-file = ?path`, kitty `include`, alacritty `[general] import`, foot `include=`) and `TerminalConfig.apply` writes the default theme files, so an include never points at nothing; your own terminal configs are never edited. The managed `hypr/bxrig.lua` reads `theme/hypr.lua` (border colours). btop needs `color_theme = "bxrig"` in your `btop.conf`, which we do not edit.
* **Not themed in v1:** the Starship prompt (fixed Catppuccin Mocha palette, no include mechanism), VS Code, Chromium, GTK and Qt apps (whether `noctalia msg templates-apply` themes them is unverified).
* **Neovim layer** (`editor lazyvim|boxlang|status|refresh`): after the starter is cloned (an existing `~/.config/nvim` is never touched) the layer is added: `lua/config/bxrig.lua` (relativenumber off, autoformat off, OSC 52 clipboard over SSH, loaded by one line added to `options.lua`), `lua/plugins/bxrig.lua` (no news popups, no scroll animation, transparent lualine), `plugin/after/bxrig-transparency.lua`, `lua/plugins/boxlang.lua` (`ortus-boxlang/vim-boxlang`, loaded at startup so its ftdetect runs first), `lua/plugins/bxrig-themes.lua` (every theme's colourscheme plugin listed lazily from `nvim-themes/`), `lua/plugins/bxrig-theme-reload.lua` (a libuv watcher re-applies the colourscheme when the theme file changes), `lua/plugins/theme.lua` (a link to the current theme's `neovim.lua`) and the neo-tree extra merged into `lazyvim.json`. It is modelled on Omarchy's `omarchy-nvim` package, written by us. `editor boxlang` adds only the plugin file to a LazyVim config you have. `refresh` rewrites the files still as BxRig wrote them and keeps the ones you changed unless `--force`.
* **Theme depth (2026-11-13):** `set` also writes `theme/tmux.conf`, `theme/fzf.sh` (FZF_DEFAULT_OPTS), `theme/rofi/theme.rasi` (plus a `rofi/config.rasi` stub only when none exists), GTK 4 and 3 `gtk.css` (libadwaita `@define-color` names, adw-gtk3 for GTK 3), qt6ct and qt5ct `colors/bxrig.conf` (21 ARGB roles), `fuzzel/fuzzel.ini` and `wofi/style.css`: 18 files in all, each kept when you edit it. It sets gsettings `color-scheme` (prefer-dark or prefer-light) and the adw-gtk3 theme when installed. `theme vscode [--yes] [--dry-run]` is opt-in: plan first (exit 2), then a plain-JSON merge into `workbench.colorCustomizations` of Code, Code - OSS, VSCodium or Cursor with a backup; a settings.json with comments or trailing commas is skipped. Exit 4 when no settings file exists. Unverified on a real desktop: that GTK, Qt, rofi, fuzzel and wofi pick the files up as written.
* **Wizard:** `theme_name` (default `bxrig`; a Light answer with the default picks `bxrig-light`) runs `theme set` after the terminals, optional, for Hyprland and Plasma; the editor answer now includes the layer and BoxLang syntax. The Themes menu has next, random, the five BxRig themes, the four modes and status.
* **Starship:** the starter prompt shows the BoxLang version like Java: `custom.boxlang` (`${custom.boxlang}` in the format), shown only in a directory with `.bx .bxs .bxm .cfc .cfm .cfs` files or `box.json`, `Application.bx`, `Application.cfc`. It has no `when` (Starship shows a custom module when ANY of `when`, `detect_files`, `detect_extensions` matches, so `when` would show it everywhere); its command prints the `~/.bvm/current` symlink name (honouring `BVM_HOME`) or nothing. The starter is written once, so existing installs see the change with `bxrig config diff starship`.

### 13.33 Virtual machines: Windows and Linux desktops in containers (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **Command:** `vm list|status [NAME]|size [NAME]|info NAME [--show-password]|doctor|versions linux|windows|create windows [NAME] [--version=V] [--ram=] [--cpus=] [--disk=] [--share=PATH|none]|create linux NAME [--tag=T] [--cpus=] [--memory=] [--share=PATH|none] [--gpu=none|auto|intel|amd|nvidia]|start|stop|logs NAME|open NAME [--web] [--fullscreen]|remove NAME [--keep-data]`, with `--json`. `create` and `remove` are plans until `--yes` (`--dry-run` too). Exit: 0 done, 2 plan or bad usage, 4 precondition (bad name or version, KVM unusable, no engine, no terminal to choose a Windows version on, GPU not possible), 6 a command failed.
* **Two kinds, any number of each.** Every VM has a name (`[a-z0-9-]`, up to 31) and a record in `~/.config/bxrig/vms/NAME.json` (mode 600). Windows is `dockurr/windows`; a Linux desktop is LinuxServer's `lscr.io/linuxserver/webtop:TAG`. The container is `bxrig-vm-NAME`, labelled `io.bxrig.vm`. The first Windows is named `windows`. The engine is the one `bxrig db engine` chose (Podman by default).
* **Where things live (documented for the user in `docs/guides/vms.md`):** data in `~/.local/share/bxrig/vms/NAME` (`storage` is the Windows disk, `config` is the Linux desktop's home folder), the record above, the password in the keyring as `BXRIG_VM_<NAME>_PASSWORD` (`bxrig secrets`), an app-menu launcher `~/.local/share/applications/bxrig-vm-NAME.desktop` (runs `vm open NAME`), and a shared folder: `~/Windows` (drive Z:) or `~/Shared` (`/config/Shared`), or `--share=none`. `remove` deletes the container, the data, the password, the record and the launcher; the shared folder is never deleted; `--keep-data` keeps data, password and record. `size` is `du` of the data folder; the images are in the engine (`podman image ls`).
* **Security:** ports bind to `127.0.0.1` only (the webtop terminal has passwordless sudo; the Windows web viewer and RDP are for you). The password is generated (16 random bytes), stored in the keyring, and reaches the container through an env file (mode 600) that is deleted right after `run`. The default `admin` password of dockur is never used.
* **Ports:** Linux 3001 upward (HTTPS, a self-signed certificate: accept it once); Windows web viewer 8006 upward and RDP 3389 upward (TCP and UDP); each VM takes the first port no record uses and nothing listens on.
* **Windows:** `--version` takes any dockur VERSION value (25, `vm versions windows`). Without it at a terminal, a picker shows ten choices with sizes and notes (11 Pro, 11 LTSC, 11 Enterprise, 10 Pro, 10 LTSC, Tiny11, Tiny11 Core, Tiny10, Server 2025 and 2022; the Tiny builds are marked UNOFFICIAL); with no terminal it exits 4 (a script passes `--version`; with `--json` the picker text goes to the terminal device, never stdout). Defaults: RAM half the machine (4G to 8G), CPUs half (2 to 8), disk 64G. Run: `--device /dev/kvm --device /dev/net/tun --cap-add NET_ADMIN --stop-timeout 120`, env `VERSION RAM_SIZE CPU_CORES DISK_SIZE USERNAME PASSWORD`. The install downloads the ISO inside the container on the first start (3 to 8 GB) and takes a while; you need your own Windows license (dockur uses generic trial keys that do not activate). `open` starts the VM if needed, waits for RDP, then runs the first FreeRDP client found (`sdl-freerdp3`, `sdl-freerdp`, `xfreerdp3`, `xfreerdp`, `wlfreerdp3`, `wlfreerdp`) with `/args-from:file:PATH`: a mode 600 file holding `/v:` `/u:` `/p:` `/cert:ignore` `+clipboard` `/dynamic-resolution` `/title:` (and `/f`), so the password is never on a command line; the file is removed after 15 seconds. While Windows is still installing, `open` says so and points at `open --web` (the browser viewer).
* **Linux:** 21 tags from the webtop page (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch: xfce, kde, mate, i3, and lxqt for Ubuntu; Alpine with the upstream `latest` tag as `alpine-xfce`); default `ubuntu-xfce`. The `dev` tag and the deprecated Enterprise Linux tags are not offered; KDE tags are Wayland only. Run: `--shm-size 1gb`, env `PUID PGID TZ CUSTOM_USER=bxrig PASSWORD`, `-v data:/config`. Rootless Podman maps the container's root to you, so PUID and PGID are 0 there (files stay yours); Docker uses your ids. `--cpus` and `--memory` map to the engine flags. When the host has no IPv6 (`/proc/sys/net/ipv6` missing) the container also gets `DISABLE_IPV6=true`, because the image's nginx otherwise fails on `listen [::]` (found by running the real image; `doctor` notes it).
* **GPU (Linux desktops, opt-in):** `intel` and `amd` add `--device /dev/dri` (needs it to exist); `auto` does that when `/dev/dri` exists and nothing otherwise; `nvidia` follows the webtop docs: Docker gets `--runtime nvidia --gpus all --device /dev/nvidia-modeset`, Podman gets CDI (`--device nvidia.com/gpu=all --device /dev/nvidia-modeset`). The Alpine tags refuse NVIDIA. `doctor` reports `/dev/dri`, the NVIDIA driver version (the docs ask for 580 or newer) and `nvidia-ctk`. Windows has no GPU option.
* **Wizard and menu:** two optional questions after the databases: `vm_windows` (none or one of the ten, with descriptions) and `vm_linux` (none or six tags); they become optional steps `vm create windows --version=V` and `vm create linux desktop --tag=T`, and add the Podman install when no engine answer was given. The menu has a Virtual machines entry (list, sizes, doctor, the two version tables).
* **Verified and not:** tested against fake Podman and Docker (every run argument, files, modes, ports, passwords, launchers, exit codes) in `tests/vm-test.sh` and `tests/init_plan_test.bxs`. **Also run for real (2026-11-13, a sandbox with Docker 29.9.2, no KVM, no IPv6, running as root):** `vm create linux` with the real `lscr.io/linuxserver/webtop:ubuntu-xfce` image through `bxrig`: the published `127.0.0.1:3001` answers 401 without credentials, 200 with the generated password and 401 with a wrong one; the shared folder works both ways; `start`, `stop`, `status`, `size`, `info`, `open` (browser launch only) and `remove` behave. **Never run:** Windows (no `/dev/kvm` here), Podman, a non-root user (so PUID and file ownership are untested), GPUs, FreeRDP. **Unverified on a real machine:** Windows booting under rootless Podman (`/dev/kvm`, `/dev/net/tun`, `NET_ADMIN`), RDP through the published `127.0.0.1` port (dockur documents the container's own IP too), dockur on a Btrfs disk (CachyOS default; not checked in its README), webtop under rootless Podman with PUID 0 and as a non-root Docker user, the NVIDIA paths (driver 580 or newer from a `.run` file per the docs, whether CachyOS's packaged driver counts, CDI on Podman, the Arch package name `nvidia-container-toolkit`), and the FreeRDP argument file (`/args-from:file:` read from the FreeRDP 3 source, the client binary names are a best guess).

### 13.34 The menu, package search and remove (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **Menu skeleton.** `bxrig menu` follows Omarchy's 11 sections and adds one of ours: Apps, Install, Remove, Appearance, Trigger, Setup, Update, **Develop** (BoxLang, databases, virtual machines, containers, the editor), Agent, Learn, About, System. What used to be top-level BxRig entries are folded in: Themes into Appearance, Notifications and Screenshot into Trigger, Cloud storage and Settings into Setup, Web apps into Install and Remove. The tree is `MenuTree` (data); `menu items [--json]` prints it, `menu search TEXT [--json]` lists the entries whose path matches with the command each runs (the CLI mirror of the in-menu search). Omarchy's menu has 362 actions; ours had 63 and now has 136 (the Appearance, Trigger, Setup, Update and System depth is still to come, see the parity plan).
* **Search.** The first entry of the top level is `Search...`: one flat list of every entry as a path ("Appearance \> Next theme"); the menu provider filters as you type, and the choice runs exactly as it would from its section.
* **Entry kinds:** `sub`, `spawn` (detached), `run` (in a terminal, waits for Enter: output and sudo prompts), `open` (xdg-open a URL), `pick` (choose from a live list, then run with `{}` replaced), `ask` (type a line, then run), `pkgsearch` (type, choose a package from the repos or the AUR, confirm, `pkg install` in a terminal), `catalog` (one catalog group, choose, confirm, `install ID --yes` in a terminal), `db`, `webcreate`, `webrm`. A `confirm` asks before running (reboot, shutdown, logout, every removal). Live lists: themes (the current one marked ✓), your themes, installed browsers, terminals and file managers, explicit packages, installed catalog apps, VMs, installed skills. Providers that cannot take typed text open a terminal that asks (`bxrig web add`) or say what to type.
* **`pkg`:** `pkg search TEXT [--source=all|repo|aur] [--limit=40]` (pacman -Ss and the AUR RPC v5 `search/TEXT?by=name-desc`; exact names first, then repo packages, then AUR by popularity; installed ones marked; an AUR outage is a note, repo results stay), `pkg info NAME`, `pkg installed [--explicit]`, `pkg install NAME... [--aur] [--yes]` (repo packages through the existing installer steps, AUR packages through `yay -S --needed --noconfirm`; never as root for the AUR, exit 4 without yay; the plan warns that AUR packages are user-submitted scripts and points at `yay -G NAME`), `pkg remove NAME... [--yes]` (`pacman -Rns --noconfirm`, one package at a time). Protected and never removed: base, pacman, sudo, systemd, glibc, bash, coreutils, filesystem, linux-firmware, grub, util-linux, shadow, the keyrings, `linux*` kernels and their headers and NVIDIA modules, and the `cachyos-settings`, `cachyos-hooks` and mirrorlist packages. Not-installed names are a no-op. Names are validated (`[a-z0-9@._+-]`), search text too.
* **`remove ID_OR_PACKAGE...`:** a catalog id removes what installing it put there (pacman, AUR and PKGBUILD apps: their targets through `pkg remove`; web apps: the launcher file); a vendor-script app is reported with exit 4 ("use its own uninstaller"); anything that is not a catalog id is taken as a package name. A plan until `--yes`; your files in `~/.config` and `~/.local` are never touched.
* **`system lock|suspend|logout|reboot|shutdown`:** through `noctalia msg session ...` inside Hyprland with Noctalia (Noctalia IPC docs), else `loginctl lock-session`, `systemctl suspend|reboot|poweroff`, `loginctl terminate-session`. Lock and suspend act at once; logout, reboot and shutdown are a plan until `--yes` (the menu asks first).
* **Verified:** `tests/pkg-test.sh` (fake pacman, yay, curl, sudo, id) and `tests/menu-test.sh` (fake Rofi, Wofi and terminal); `pkg search|info|install|remove` and `remove` were also run against the real Arch repos and the live AUR in the Arch test container (search, install and remove of `cowsay`, `jq` removed by catalog id, protected packages refused). **Not verified:** the menu on a real provider (Rofi, Walker, Fuzzel), AUR installs through `yay`, `system` actions on a real session.

The plan states the privacy tradeoff: GeoClue looks up your location online (Wi-Fi networks or IP address).

### 13.39 Toggles, DNS, kernels and security (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **`bxrig toggle stay-awake [on|off]`** runs `noctalia msg caffeine-enable|disable|toggle` (Noctalia IPC docs). Without Noctalia it exits 4 (on Plasma use System Settings \> Power Management). Noctalia has no screensaver, so there is no screensaver toggle; `notify dnd|snooze` already cover reminders.
* **`bxrig dns [cloudflare|google|quad9|dhcp|custom IP[,IP...]]`** lists or sets the DNS servers of the active NetworkManager connections (loopback, bridge, tunnel and container devices are skipped) with `nmcli connection modify NAME ipv4.dns ... ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes ipv6.dns ... ipv6.ignore-auto-dns yes`, then `connection up NAME`. `dhcp` clears them. A plan (exit 2) without `--yes`; a bad IP exits 2.
* **`bxrig kernel list|install NAME|remove NAME`.** `list` shows the running kernel, the installed kernel packages and the `linux-cachyos*` kernels you could add (nvidia, zfs, rc and headers packages are left out). `install` is `sudo pacman -S --needed NAME NAME-headers` (the name must match `linux(-[a-z0-9]+)*` and exist in the repos, else exit 4 or 2). `remove` refuses the running kernel (judged from `uname -r` and the package suffix) and the last installed kernel (exit 4). It never edits the bootloader and never picks the default: the boot entries come from the kernel packages' hooks and you choose in the boot menu.
* **`bxrig security status|fingerprint|fido2|ssh-server|passwordless-sudo`.** Guards: only `/etc/pam.d/sudo` is ever changed (never login, SDDM or the lock screen); the line is `auth sufficient pam_fprintd.so` or `auth sufficient pam_u2f.so cue` inserted before the first `auth` line and marked with a `# bxrig KIND` comment, so your password still works without the reader or key; a file with no `auth` line is left alone (exit 4); the original is kept once as `/etc/pam.d/sudo.bxrig-backup`; `off` removes exactly the marked line; running `on` twice adds one line. `fingerprint enroll` runs `fprintd-enroll`; `fido2 register` runs `pamu2fcfg` into `~/.config/Yubico/u2f_keys`, and `fido2 on` refuses (exit 4) until that file exists. `passwordless-sudo on` writes `/etc/sudoers.d/50-bxrig-nopasswd` (`USER ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL`, user from ``$USER` and checked against `^[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]*$``) only after `visudo -cf` passes, with mode 440; `off` removes it. `ssh-server on|off` installs openssh and runs `systemctl enable|disable --now sshd.service`. Everything is a plan (exit 2) without `--yes`, and `--dry-run` prints the exact line or file.
* **Agents:** the Agent menu runs `ai launch NAME`; there is no separate `agent` command.
* **Menu:** Trigger \> Toggle (stay awake), Setup \> DNS, Security, Time, Kernel. **Verified:** `tests/tweaks-test.sh` and `tests/security-test.sh` (fake nmcli, pacman, noctalia, uname, visudo, sudo and fake `/etc/pam.d` and `/etc/sudoers.d`). Not verified on a real machine: PAM behavior with a real reader or key, `nmcli` on your connection names, kernel removal.

### 13.40 The command reference and `bxrig help` (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **One source:** `docs/reference/cli.json` holds, for every command, its group, a one-sentence summary, its usage lines, examples, whether it needs `--yes` (`mutates`) and an optional note. `bootstrap/gen-docs.sh` writes `docs/reference/commands.md` (the docs page: flags, exit codes, the JSON envelope, an index by group, then every command with usage and examples) and `src/bxrig/HelpData.bx` (the same data inside the binary).
* **`bxrig help`** (and bare `bxrig`) lists every command by group with its summary; `bxrig help NAME` prints the summary, usage, whether `--yes` is needed, examples and notes; `--json` returns the same data; an unknown name exits 2.
* **Drift checks:** `gen-docs.sh --check` fails when a command in `src/Main.bx` has no entry, an entry has no command, a usage line does not start with its command, an example names no real command, a summary does not end in a full stop, or the text contains an em dash. The usage lines of older commands are copied from the usage text in `src/Main.bx`; the newer classes (`appearance`, `display`, `power`, `time`, `toggle`, `dns`, `kernel`, `security`) print their own usage, so their entries are written by hand and must be updated with the class.
* **Verified:** `tests/help-test.sh` (the groups, a command, JSON, unknown, and that the generated files are current).

### 13.41 NAS as a first-class namespace (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **`bxrig nas`** keeps every NAS you use in `~/.config/bxrig/nas.json` (name, host, protocol `smb` or `nfs`, user, optional SMB version, and the shares you mounted). `discover` browses the network with `avahi-browse -rtp _smb._tcp` and `_nfs._tcp` (IPv4 only). `setup` installs `cifs-utils nfs-utils smbclient avahi nss-mdns rsync` and enables `avahi-daemon` (a plan without `--yes`; every tool was checked in the Arch repos and its binary exists after install).
* **`add NAME --host=H`** needs `--user` and a password for SMB (`--ask-password`, typed hidden, or `--password-file=F`); the password goes to the keyring as `BXRIG_NAS_<NAME>_PASSWORD` and never into `nas.json`. NFS needs neither. Names are `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$`.
* **`shares NAME`** lists SMB shares with `smbclient -g -L HOST -A AUTHFILE` (the auth file is a private temp file, deleted after; no password on a command line; `IPC$` and other hidden shares are dropped) or NFS exports with `showmount -e --no-headers`.
* **`mount|unmount NAME SHARE`** mounts at `~/NAS/NAME/LEAF` (`BXRIG_NAS_HOME` overrides) with `sudo mount -t cifs|nfs`; the SMB options are `credentials=/etc/bxrig/nas/NAME.cred,uid,gid,iocharset=utf8,file_mode=0600,dir_mode=0700` plus `vers=` only when you set one (otherwise the kernel negotiates the highest version both sides support). **The credentials file is root-only (mode 600) because `mount.cifs` reads it as root**; the plan says so.
* **`auto on|off NAME SHARE`** writes `<escaped-path>.mount` and `.automount` units to `/etc/systemd/system` (`Options=...,nofail`, `TimeoutSec=20`, `TimeoutIdleSec=600`, wanted by `multi-user.target`), runs `daemon-reload` and `enable --now`, so a sleeping NAS never blocks login. `off` disables and removes them; a NAS with automatic mounts is not removed (exit 4) until they are off.
* **`test NAME [SHARE]`** checks: reachable (TCP 445 or 2049), signed in or exports readable, mounted (`findmnt`), writable (a probe file), free space. Exit 4 when a check fails.
* **`sync NAME SRC --to=SHARE[/PATH]`** is a plain `rsync -a` mirror to a mounted share. Nothing is deleted from the NAS unless you add `--delete`, and the plan says so in capitals.
* **`use NAME SHARE [--path=bxrig-backup]`** records `targets.nas-NAME` in `~/.config/bxrig/backup.json` (`{type: nas, nas, share, path}`); `backup data setup` reads it.
* **Verified:** `tests/nas-test.sh` with fake avahi-browse, smbclient, showmount, findmnt, rsync, sudo and a fake `/etc`. **Not verified on a real Synology:** DSM share permissions, SMB signing, NFS export options, `nss-mdns` name resolution.

### 13.42 `refresh` and `reinstall` (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **No factory reset.** `bxrig refresh COMPONENT` puts managed config back to what BxRig ships and never installs a package. Components: `hyprland` (runs `keys apply`, `appearance apply`, `display apply`; with `--starter` also the starter `hyprland.lua`), `noctalia` (`theme set CURRENT`, `appearance apply`, `noctalia msg config-reload`; with `--starter` also the Noctalia starter files), `terminals` (the starter config of each installed terminal, then the theme includes), `shell` (`starship.toml`, the shell init and the line in `.zshrc` or `.bashrc`), `nvim` (`editor refresh`), `theme` (`theme set CURRENT`, `appearance apply`), `all`, and `list`.
* **Semantics are the config service's:** a clean file is left alone, a missing or outdated one is written, a file you edited (`drifted`) is kept and reported, and `--force` overwrites it after a backup (`config history`, `config restore`). A link or special file in the way blocks (exit 8 in the service, shown as blocked). Without `--yes` it prints the plan and exits 2; `--dry-run` exits 0.
* **`reinstall`** is `init --rerun`: the way to install packages again.
* **Verified:** `tests/refresh-test.sh` (temp home, fake `bxrig` that logs the commands, a fake terminal): plan and dry run write nothing, files are written, a second run rewrites nothing clean, edits are kept, `--force` overwrites and takes a backup, each component runs its commands.

### 13.43 Backups: the config layer (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **Three layers, one command.** `bxrig backup config` (your BxRig setup), `backup snapshots` (the system, Btrfs with snapper) and `backup data` (your files, restic) are built in that order; `backup send` and `backup export` move any of them, and `timemachine` shows them all. This section is the config layer; the others are added below as they land.

* **A snapshot** is `~/.local/share/bxrig/backups/config/ID.tar.gz` (mode 600) plus `ID.json`. `ID` is `yyyyMMddTHHmmss` (with `-xxxx` when two land in the same second). Inside: `files/` (paths under your home), `packages.txt` (`pacman -Qqe`), `foreign.txt` (`pacman -Qqm`), `meta.json`, and `secrets.bxs` only with `--with-secrets` (the output of `bxrig secrets export`, encrypted with a passphrase you type).

* **What is tracked** (under your home): `.config/bxrig`, `hypr`, `noctalia`, `ghostty`, `kitty`, `foot`, `alacritty`, `starship.toml`, `nvim`, `btop`, `fish`, `git`, `mimeapps.list`, `xdg-terminals.list`, `.zshrc`, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.ssh/config`. `backup config add|remove PATH` changes the list (stored in `backup.json`); SSH keys, `gnupg`, `..` and absolute paths are refused. `.git`, `node_modules` and `*.log` are skipped.

* **Restore** shows a plan (which files are created or replaced; exit 2 without `--yes`), takes a **safety snapshot of the present** first, then copies the files back (`--only=PATH` limits it). `--packages` installs the explicit packages that are missing and exist in the repositories with `sudo pacman -S --needed --noconfirm`; AUR and local ones are listed for `yay`, never installed from here. `diff ID` compares a snapshot with now (files same, changed, missing, and missing packages).

* **Automatic:** `auto` is on by default. Before `update apply`, `system update`, `init`, `reinstall` and `refresh` (with `--yes`, never `--dry-run`) a snapshot is taken quietly, with the reason `before <command>`; it never stops the command. The newest 30 are kept (`prune --keep=N`).

* **Verified:** `tests/backup-config-test.sh` (temp home, fake pacman, sudo and bxrig). Not verified: a restore on a different machine.

* **`backup snapshots`** (system snapshots). Btrfs root: snapper. `setup [--home]` installs `snapper snap-pac` (and `grub-btrfs` only when GRUB is in use), creates the `root` config (`snapper -c root create-config /`; `--home` adds `/home`), sets the timeline to 5 hourly, 7 daily, 2 weekly, 1 monthly, 0 yearly (`snapper set-config TIMELINE_*`), and enables `snapper-timeline.timer` and `snapper-cleanup.timer` (and `grub-btrfsd.service`). snap-pac takes a snapshot before and after every pacman transaction through its own hooks. Other filesystems: it installs Timeshift (rsync mode), which takes full copies and needs one visit to its window to pick a disk. `list` reads `snapper --jsonout -c CONFIG list` (snapshot 0, the live system, is left out); `create [--description=T]` is `snapper create --description T -p`; `delete ID`; `changes ID` is `snapper status ID..0`; `restore ID PATH` is `snapper undochange ID..0 PATH` (files changed since are replaced, files that did not exist then are removed, so the plan says so). **There is no automatic whole-system rollback** : rolling back a Btrfs root depends on your subvolume layout, so you boot the snapshot from the GRUB menu and follow the Arch wiki, or restore folders with `restore`. Everything that changes the system is a plan without `--yes`. **Not verified on real Btrfs:** the JSON shape of `snapper --jsonout list` (the parser accepts a bare array or an object holding one array), the timers, `undochange`. Tested with fakes in `tests/backup-snapshots-test.sh`.

* **`backup data`** (your files, restic). A **target** is a place a restic repository lives: `local` (a path), `nas` (made by `nas use`, at `~/NAS/NAME/SHARE/PATH`), `sftp` (`sftp:user@host:/path`; port as `sftp:-p N user@host:/path`), `rest` (`rest:URL`), `s3` (`s3:ENDPOINT/BUCKET/PATH`, AWS when no endpoint; works for DigitalOcean Spaces, Wasabi, MinIO), `b2` (`b2:BUCKET:PATH`), `azure` (`azure:CONTAINER:/PATH`), `gs` (`gs:BUCKET:/PATH`, with `GOOGLE_PROJECT_ID` and `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` as the project and the service-account file) and `rclone` (`rclone:REMOTE:PATH`; FTP and any rclone service). The environment variable names (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, `B2_ACCOUNT_ID`, `B2_ACCOUNT_KEY`, `AZURE_ACCOUNT_NAME`, `AZURE_ACCOUNT_KEY`, `RESTIC_REST_USERNAME`, `RESTIC_REST_PASSWORD`) and the address forms were read from restic's own documentation; the flags used (`-r` via `RESTIC_REPOSITORY`, `backup --tag --exclude --exclude-caches --one-file-system`, `forget --keep-daily|weekly|monthly --prune`, `snapshots --json`, `ls --json`, `restore --target --include`, `check --read-data-subset`) from the installed restic 0.19.1.

  * **Keys go straight to the keyring** (`target add ... --ask-keys`, typed hidden, or `--keys-file` with `KEY=VALUE` lines) as `BXRIG_BACKUP_<TARGET>_<KEY>`; the **repository password is generated at `init`** (24 random bytes, hex) and kept as `BXRIG_BACKUP_<TARGET>_PASSWORD`, with a reminder that losing it loses the backups. restic is started with these in its **environment** , never on a command line, and no key is written to `backup.json`.
  * `run` backs up the include list (default `Projects code dev Documents .ssh`, only the ones that exist) skipping the exclude list (default `node_modules target .gradle __pycache__ .venv venv .cache .next *.tmp`) and cache folders, on one filesystem, tagged `bxrig`; `list`, `files`, `restore ID --to=DIR [--include=PATH]` (into a folder you name, never over your files by itself), `verify [--deep]` (`restic check`, `--read-data-subset 5%`), `forget` (retention 7 daily, 4 weekly, 6 monthly by default, `retention` changes it; deletes older backups for good, so it is a plan first), `schedule hourly|daily|off` (user units `bxrig-backup.service` and `.timer`: `ConditionACPower=true` so it skips on battery, `Persistent=true` to catch up, a random delay up to 15 minutes; a failed scheduled run sends a Noctalia or `notify-send` notification). An unmounted NAS share exits 4 with the `nas mount` command.
  * **Verified:** `tests/backup-data-test.sh` with a fake restic that records its arguments and the variables it was given. **Not verified against a real cloud account, NAS or restic repository** in this environment.
* **`backup send` and `backup export`** (moving backups). `send ID|all --to=TARGET [--from=TARGET]` is `restic copy` into a second repository (a NAS and a cloud bucket, for a 3-2-1 setup): the destination is `RESTIC_REPOSITORY`, the source goes in `RESTIC_FROM_REPOSITORY` with `RESTIC_FROM_PASSWORD_COMMAND=printenv BXRIG_FROM_PW`, so no password is on a command line. restic reads one set of `AWS_*`, `B2_*` ... variables, so two repositories that need different values for the same variable (two S3 accounts) are refused (exit 4) with a pointer to `rclone sync`. `export data ID --to=FILE` is `restic dump --archive tar|zip --target FILE ID PATH` (zip when the name ends in `.zip`; `--path` limits it to a folder; an existing file is never overwritten), `export config ID --to=FILE.tar.gz` copies a config snapshot out as one file. **Config snapshots travel with the data backups** : `~/.local/share/bxrig/backups/config` is in the default include list, so a NAS or cloud target protects them with no extra step. System snapshots are not exportable. Tested in `tests/backup-move-test.sh` with a fake restic.

### 13.44 BxTimeMachine, the backup screen (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **`bxrig timemachine [--demo] [--local]`** (also `bxrig bxtimemachine`) is **BxTimeMachine** , a full-screen terminal UI on MatchBox's canvas (the same one as the wizard) over **`bxrig backup timeline [--json] [--local]`** , which lists every backup in one structure: rows `system` (snapper), `config` (config snapshots), `files-NAME` (one per data target, from `restic snapshots --json`) and `mirror-NAME` (recorded `nas sync` runs). A point is `{ id, time, epoch, label, tier, size }`; **tier** is by age (hourly up to a day, daily to a week, weekly to 5 weeks, monthly to a year, yearly after). A target that fails is a row with an `error` (unreachable, not initialized, NAS not mounted), never a failure of the whole timeline; `--local` leaves out the targets that need the network so the screen opens at once. `BXRIG_TIMELINE_FILE` injects a timeline (tests); `BXRIG_NOW_EPOCH` fixes the clock.
* **The screen:** places as rows over a time axis (newest on the right; zoom 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 1 year, all; the axis grows to keep the chosen backup in view), points coloured by tier, a guide line through the chosen moment, the chosen backup as a card with the older ones stacked behind it, counts by tier for the place, and the brand gradient with Powered by BoxLang. Keys: left and right (or h l) through time, up and down (k j) between places, plus and minus zoom, enter open, d diff, r restore, e export, s send, n back up now, / filter in the browser, ? help, q or esc leave; the mouse picks a point, a place or a zoom chip and the wheel moves through time. Under 90 by 30 cells it asks for a bigger window.
* **What it runs:** it only runs `bxrig` commands, and **every change goes through a plan first** : it runs the command with `--dry-run`, shows the plan, and runs it with `--yes` only on `y`. Open: `backup data files ID --json`, `backup config show ID --json` or `backup snapshots changes N`. Restore: `backup data restore ID --to=~/Restored/ID [--include=PATH]`, `backup config restore ID [--only=PATH]` or `backup snapshots restore N PATH` (a folder must be picked first). Export: `backup export data|config`. Send: `backup send ID --from=PLACE --to=PLACE` (file backups only; a destination picker). Back up now: `backup data run`, `backup config now` or `backup snapshots create`. Config snapshots reach a NAS or the cloud through the data backups (they are in its include list).
* **`--demo`** shows a made-up timeline (every kind of place and every tier) and runs nothing: plans and results say what the command would have been. `tools/record-timemachine.py` records the demo in a pseudo-terminal (pyte, Pillow, ffmpeg) into named screenshots and a video.
* **Verified:** `tests/time_machine_test.bxs` (the model, the keys and intents, the date maths, and what each screen shows via `render_to_string`) and `tests/timeline-test.sh`. **Not yet tried:** against real restic repositories, a real NAS or snapper on Btrfs; with a real terminal beyond the recorded demo.

### 13.45 The backup pages of the wizard (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* The wizard has three pages after Containers, in this order: **NAS** (`nas_use`, `nas_name`, `nas_host`, `nas_protocol`, `nas_user`, `nas_share`, `nas_auto`), **Remote backups** (`remote_type` none, s3, b2, azure, gs, sftp, rclone or local, with `remote_name`, `remote_endpoint`, `remote_bucket`, `remote_region`, `remote_container`, `remote_project`, `remote_credentials`, `remote_host`, `remote_user`, `remote_remote`, `remote_path`) and **Backups** (`backup_layers`: config, snapshots, data; `backup_schedule`: daily, hourly, off). The old tools-only `backups` question is gone; `restic` is installed when files are protected.
* **No secret is in an answer.** The plan steps are commands that ask for them in the terminal while the setup runs: `nas add ... --ask-password` (SMB) and `backup data target add ... --ask-keys` (S3, B2, Azure). Every NAS, target and schedule step is optional, so a missing network or a wrong password never stops the rest of the plan. Steps in order: `nas-setup`, `nas-add`, `nas-mount`, `nas-auto`, `nas-use`; `backup-remote`; per place `backup-init-PLACE`, `backup-default`, `backup-schedule`; `backup-snapshots`; `backup-config-off` when the config layer is not chosen.
* `backup data run --all` (used by the schedule) backs up every place that is set up; `backup data default NAME` chooses the place used without `--target`.
* **Verified:** `tests/init_plan_test.bxs` (the steps for a Synology over SMB, NFS, S3, Google, a disk, a missing address) and the wizard tests (13 pages in Basic mode).

### 13.46 The TUI kit and the Control Center (decided with the owner 2026-11-13)

* **Kit** (`TuiKit`, `TuiList`, `TuiRunner`): every terminal screen paints with one kit (palette, text, gradient, panels, click regions, tabs, scrolling list, modal and plan box, toast, key bar, meter, badge, sparkline), keeps list state in `TuiList` (cursor, scroll, filter) and runs through `TuiRunner` (one loop that always restores the terminal). The wizard and BxTimeMachine use it; their tests did not change.
* **Command:** `tui [PAGE] [--demo] [--json]`. Without `--json` it needs a terminal (exit 4 without one). `--json` prints the page's data (`{ data, attention, cursor }`) and exits 0; an unknown page or more than one word exits 2. `--demo` uses made-up data and runs nothing.
* **Page interface:** a class with `id() title() load() keys() paint( kit, x, y, w, h, tick, phase ) onKey( key ) act( hit ) onScroll( dir )`. A key, click or scroll returns an intent: `{}`, `{ action: "goto", page }`, `{ action: "launch", target }` (leave and run that screen, then come back to the same page) or `{ action: "cli", title, args }`. A `cli` intent first runs the command with `--dry-run` and shows the output as the plan; only `y` runs it with `--yes`, and the result box follows.
* **Keys:** Tab and Shift+Tab (or `]` and `[`) change page, Left moves to the sidebar, Right or Enter returns, q, Escape and Ctrl+c leave.
* **Dashboard** (built): needs attention (updates from `checkupdates` when installed, backups older than 2 days or none, disk 85% or more, battery 20% or less and not charging), system meters (`/proc`, `df`, `/sys/class/power_supply`, `BXRIG_POWER_DIR`), machines (`db list --json` and `vm list --json`) and backups (the timeline, `--local`). Every part is read alone; a part that fails is left out. `BXRIG_DASHBOARD_FILE` (a JSON file) replaces the machine for tests.
* **Table pages** (`ListPage` with a provider: `id title columns load( query ) actions detail style hint live emptyText`): BoxLang (`bvm list`, `bvm current`, read leniently: every version number on a line, a `*` or `(current)` marks the active one; unverified against a working bvm), Java (`bxrig java list`), Versions (BoxLang, MatchBox, Java, Node; Enter opens the deep page), Ports (`ss -ltnpH` and `ps`; one row per port and pid; two owners on a port is a conflict), Packages (live `pkg search`), Shortcuts (`keys show`), Machines (VMs only: `vm list`), Databases (`db list`), Storage (`nas list`, `cloud status`), Secrets (`secrets list`, a value only through `secrets get --show`), Themes (`theme list`) and Logs (`journalctl -b -o json -p`, priority cycles error, warning, info). Keys compare exactly (`K` is not `k`). While a page takes text (a filter or a search) it gets every key, including q and Escape.
* **More intents:** `{ action: "exec", title, argv, plan }` (a plan you wrote, then the program), `{ action: "show", title, args }` (run `bxrig ARGS` at once and show the output; only for reads), `{ action: "ask", title, prompt, make }` (a text box; `make( value )` returns the next intent) and `{ action: "reload" }`.
* **Icons** (2026-11-14): `TuiKit.icon( name )` returns a Nerd Font glyph (Font Awesome range, plus `e738` for Java; all checked against the Symbols Nerd Font) or `""` when icons are off. Pages say which icon they use with `icon()`. `tui --icons=on|off` and `BXRIG_ICONS` decide; otherwise a Nerd Font found by `fc-list` turns them on. No emoji: their width differs between terminals and breaks the cell layout.
* **Not built yet:** BxTimeMachine inside the sidebar (it opens full screen and returns), `mise` and `nvm` actions, rebinding with a key-capture.
* **Known MatchBox quirk:** reading a missing key of a parsed JSON struct inside a try block in a nested function panicked the native runner while the interpreter did not; the code checks the key first. To be reproduced and reported upstream.

### 13.47 Java, Maven and Gradle (decided with the owner 2026-11-14)

* **`bxrig java`** (`Java.bx`): `list|available|install MAJOR|default ID|MAJOR [--unset]|remove ID|env [ID]`. Homes: `~/.local/share/bxrig/java/ID` (BxRig's own Temurin installs from the Adoptium API: `/v3/info/available_releases` and `/v3/binary/latest/MAJOR/ga/linux/x64/jdk/hotspot/normal/eclipse`, both checked), SDKMAN (`~/.sdkman/candidates/java`) and `/usr/lib/jvm`. Only BxRig's own installs are removed. The default is `java.sh` and `java.fish` in `~/.config/bxrig`, sourced by the three shell starters. Install and default and remove plan first (exit 2 without `--yes`). Overrides for tests: `BXRIG_JAVA_DIR`, `BXRIG_JAVA_SYSTEM_DIR`, `BXRIG_SDKMAN_DIR`, `BXRIG_ADOPTIUM_API`, `BXRIG_JAVA_DOWNLOAD_URL`.
* **`bxrig sdk`** (`Sdk.bx`, decided 2026-11-14: SDKMAN is the way to install Java, Maven and Gradle): `status|setup|list C|available C|install C V|default C V|remove C V`, C is java, maven or gradle. Checked against the real SDKMAN: the version lists come from `api.sdkman.io/2/candidates/CAND/linuxx64/versions/list` (Java is a vendor table, `| Vendor | Use | Version | Identifier |`; Maven and Gradle are columns that run down, read column by column) and `/candidates/default/CAND`; the installer is `get.sdkman.io?rcupdate=false`, which leaves `.bashrc` and `.zshrc` alone; commands run in `bash -c` with `SDKMAN_DIR` exported and `sdk` loaded from `bin/sdkman-init.sh`; `sdk install` gets `n` on stdin (the first install becomes the default by itself, a later one does not), `remove` is `sdk uninstall`. Versions are checked against `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9.+_-]*$` and passed as arguments, never in the script text. Maven and Gradle reach shells through `sdk.sh` and `sdk.fish` (PATH and `MAVEN_HOME`, `GRADLE_HOME` pointing at each `current` link); Java stays with `java.sh`. `java install` uses SDKMAN when it is installed (a major picks the newest Temurin, an identifier is passed on) and the direct Adoptium download otherwise; `java remove` of a SDKMAN home runs `sdk uninstall`. Overrides for tests: `BXRIG_SDKMAN_DIR`, `BXRIG_SDKMAN_API`, `BXRIG_SDKMAN_INSTALLER`.

### 13.48 The mail catcher (decided with the owner 2026-11-14)

* **Command:** `mail start [--keep] [--smtp-port=N] [--ui-port=N] [--yes] [--dry-run]|stop|status|remove [--keep-data] [--yes]|list [--limit=N]|show ID|delete ID [--yes]|clear [--yes]|open [ID]|test [--to=ADDR] [--subject=TEXT]|env [--json]`. A development inbox: Mailpit (`axllent/mailpit`) in a container named `bxrig-mail`, SMTP on `127.0.0.1:1025`, web inbox and REST API on `127.0.0.1:8025` (both ports can be changed; ports are 1024 to 65535 and must differ, else exit 4). Everything is bound to `127.0.0.1`. The engine is the one `db engine` chose (podman by default).
* **Thrown away on stop.** Without `--keep` the container runs with `--rm` and no volume, so `stop` deletes it and its mail. With `--keep` it runs with `--restart unless-stopped`, the folder `~/.local/share/bxrig/mail` bind-mounted at `/data:Z` and `MP_DATABASE=/data/mailpit.db`, so mail survives stop and start. `remove` deletes the container and the stored mail; `--keep-data` keeps the folder. `start`, `remove`, `clear` and `delete` plan first (exit 2 without `--yes`, `--dry-run` exits 0); `test`, `open`, `list`, `show`, `env`, `stop` and `status` act at once. The ports and `keep` are remembered in `mail/meta.json`.
* **Container settings:** `MP_SMTP_AUTH_ACCEPT_ANY=1`, `MP_SMTP_AUTH_ALLOW_INSECURE=1` (an app that logs in works with any user and password, no TLS) and `MP_MAX_MESSAGES=5000`, taken from Mailpit's own Docker example.
* **API used** (from Mailpit's swagger): `GET /api/v1/messages?limit=N` (`total`, `unread`, `messages[]` with `ID`, `From{Name,Address}`, `To[]`, `Subject`, `Created`, `Size`, `Attachments` as a count, `Read`, `Snippet`), `GET /api/v1/message/{ID}` (`Text`, `HTML`, `Cc`, `Bcc`, `Date`, `Attachments[]` with `FileName`, `ContentType`, `Size`), `DELETE /api/v1/messages` (all, or a body `{ "IDs": [...] }`), `POST /api/v1/send` (`From{Email,Name}`, `To[{Email}]`, `Subject`, `Text`) and `GET /view/{ID}.html` (opened with `xdg-open`). HTTP goes through `curl`. Without an answer, anything that needs the API exits 4.
* **JSON names differ from the API's on purpose** (`mid`, `sender`, `sender_address`, `recipient`, `subject_line`, `received`, `bytes`, `attachment_count`, `seen`, `preview`; for `show`: `to_list`, `cc_list`, `bcc_list`, `sent`, `body_text`, `body_html`, `files[]` with `file_name`, `type`, `bytes`; for `test`: `recipient`, `subject_line`): MatchBox keeps the capitalisation of the first spelling of a key it sees, so a field called `id` came out as `ID` after parsing the API's `ID`. Fields that do not clash (`total`, `unread`, `smtp`, `web`) keep their names.
* **`mail env`** prints the SMTP settings (host, port, no encryption, no login needed) for a generic list, BoxLang and ColdBox (words only: the exact setting names were not checked), Laravel (`.env`), Spring Boot, Node (nodemailer) and plain environment variables.
* **Control Center page `Mail`:** table of from, received, size, attachment mark and subject; the detail box shows the headers and the wrapped text body of the highlighted message. `d` plans `mail delete ID`, `c` plans `mail clear`, `o` runs `mail open ID` at once, `t` runs `mail test`, `r` reloads. The page reloads itself every 3 seconds (the provider's `refreshSeconds()`; `ListPage` reloads in `paint` once enough ticks have passed, not while you are typing a filter, and keeps the cursor on the same message by its `id`). Providers can also say `detailLines()` (default 2) to get a taller detail box. Demo data under `tui mail --demo`.
* **Wizard and menu:** one yes or no question `mail_catcher` (default no) after the databases questions; InitPlan adds the optional step `mail-start` (`bxrig mail start --yes`), so a missing container engine never stops the plan. Menu: Develop \> Mail catcher.
* **Unverified (no container engine here):** a real Mailpit container starting from these arguments (bind mount ownership under rootless podman, the `:Z` label on non-SELinux hosts, whether Mailpit creates `mailpit.db` in the mounted folder), the Mailpit version's exact response fields beyond the swagger, and the BoxLang and ColdBox mail setting names. Tests use a fake container engine and a local fake of the API paths.

### 13.49 The rename to BxRig (decided with the owner 2026-11-14)

* **Supported today:** CachyOS and Arch Linux. Other distributions (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora) are the direction, not yet supported.
* **Why:** the project is not tied to CachyOS or to Arch, so it is named BxRig. It had not been released under the old name, so this is a plain rename and the old names are gone.
* **One-liner (everywhere):** "BxRig brings an opinionated, beautiful and efficient desktop to Linux, built for developers." Longer: "BxRig turns a fresh Linux install into a polished developer rig: a themed desktop, the languages and tools you use, and one terminal screen to manage it all." Tagline: "Your dev rig. Beautiful by default."
* **Names:** `bxrig` (the binary, `dist/bxrig`, the class folder `src/bxrig`), `BXRIG_*` (environment), `~/.config/bxrig`, `~/.local/state/bxrig`, `~/.local/share/bxrig`, `~/Pictures/BxRig`, themes `bxrig`, `bxrig-light`, `bxrig-midnight`, `bxrig-cyan`, `bxrig-forest`, skills `bxrig`, `bxrig-ai`, `bxrig-apps`, `bxrig-desktop`, `bxrig-install-update`, `bxrig-system`, systemd units and launchers `bxrig-*`, containers `bxrig-*` with labels `io.bxrig.*`, the Hyprland module `bxrig.lua`, the keyring service `bxrig`, release assets `bxrig-linux-x86_64` and the S3 folder `ortussolutions/bxrig/`. BxTimeMachine keeps its name.
* **Brand:** `Brand.bx` holds the logo art (large 7 rows, small 3 rows, one line) and the descriptions; `TuiKit.logo( x, y, size, phase, bg )` paints it with the brand gradient (cyan #00DBFF to green #00FF78). It is on the wizard welcome screen, the Control Center sidebar and dashboard header, the BxTimeMachine header, `version` and `help` at a terminal (24-bit colour unless `NO_COLOR`), and the installer banner. `docs/brand/bxrig-ascii.txt` shows every size; `assets/build.py` draws the mark (a rounded gradient box with Bx) for the icon, the logo and the four wallpapers.
* **Care taken in the rename:** a few places measured the old name with a hard-coded length (`left( f, 14 )` for `bxcachy-cloud-`, the `X-BxRig-Web=` key, the settings archive prefix, the theme origin test); they were found by the test suite and now use the new lengths.
* **Intentionally still named bxcachy:** the MatchBox integration branch `bxcachy` (`box.json` `ref`, `scripts/dev-build.sh`, `scripts/get-matchbox.sh`, the matchbox workflow and its S3 folder `ortussolutions/bxcachy/matchbox`: they belong to the MatchBox repository and the owner's bucket); the docs domain `bxcachy.boxlang.io` (the owner moves it); the legacy reference tree `artifacts/legacy/` and `plan.md` history (records of what was). The word CachyOS is factual and stays. The local directory `/home/user/bxcachy` is unchanged.
* **Only the owner can:** point DNS and the docs CNAME at the new domain; check the renamed repository's settings and secrets (the signing secret is `BXRIG_SIGNING_KEY`); rotate the release signing key if wanted; create the S3 folder and CDN paths; move the MatchBox branch and its S3 folder; claim package-registry names; rename the local checkout.

## 14. Install and the setup wizard (decided with the owner 2026-11-10; install, wizard and the init engine are built, the pages' later commands are not)

### 14.1 Install

`bootstrap/install.sh [--yes] [--dry-run]` is the one install command. It prints the plan, asks one `Proceed? [Y/n]` at a terminal (without a terminal it needs `--yes`, else exit 2; `--dry-run` exits 0), then runs, in order: packages with yay and Rust, toolchains (mvm, bvm, BoxLang, nvm and Node, MatchBox), the bxrig binary, and the core apps (`bxrig profile-install core --yes`). External installer scripts run without a gate (section 2, rule 8). `install.sh check` is the read-only report; `packages|toolchains|binary|core --yes` re-run one stage. When the wizard exists the install ends by starting it at a terminal.

**Required vs optional toolchains (decided 2026-11-10):** the install always adds BoxLang (Java 21, bvm, mvm, MatchBox, Rust). nvm and Node.js are no longer part of it; they are the optional JavaScript toolchain: `bxrig toolchain node [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]` runs the pinned nvm installer from `box.json` `toolchain.nvm` (an external script: its URL is in the plan, it adds nvm to your shell startup files) and `nvm install lts/*`, skipping what is already there. Bun and Deno are catalog apps (`install bun deno`).

### 14.2 `bxrig init`

A full-screen terminal wizard that asks the questions below, shows a review screen, then runs the matching commands. Answers are saved to `~/.config/bxrig/answers.json` (mode 600, written atomically); a re-run starts from the saved answers.

    bxrig init                          the wizard (needs a terminal)
    bxrig init --answers FILE [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]    headless: no TUI, the plan from FILE; same --yes / --dry-run rules as every mutating verb
    bxrig init --print-answers          the saved answers

Exits: as `setup` (0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8); 4 also for no terminal without `--answers`. The wizard is only a front end: every answer becomes an ordinary command, so anything it does can be run by hand.

The login session follows the choice: `hyprland` starts Hyprland, `plasma` starts Plasma, and `both` asks (`login_session`, default Hyprland). `session set` runs for the resulting session. A question may carry `when: { id, in: [...] }` (or `equals`); hidden questions are not asked, not reviewed and not in the answers file.

Apps: Basic runs `install --shell=...`; Customize runs one `install` with the ticked apps (filtered by desktop); then `default browser` and `default terminal`. ### 14.4 Rules

* Every answer is optional; an unanswered page does nothing. The review screen lists exactly the commands that will run.
* `init` never runs a step the user did not choose, and never overwrites a file the user changed (the config service rules of section 6 apply).
* Starter configs are parametrized by the answers (workspaces, window style, layouts, theme, wallpaper, bar position, world clocks, natural scroll); the defaults are the current starters.
* Databases follow the earlier plan (`plan.md` section 7): Podman is the default engine and Docker is an explicit choice; services run as containers with start, stop, status and logs, persistent volumes and generated passwords kept in a mode-600 file.
* Runner integration (legacy `bxrig-runner`): launcher providers `system`, `noctalia`, `rofi`, `walker`, `krunner`, `vicinae`, `hyprrunner`, `custom`; menu providers `rofi`, `walker`, `vicinae`, `hyprrunner`; commands are JSON argument arrays, never shell strings; keybindings are never changed. Default on Hyprland is Noctalia (Super+Space).
* The TUI needs MatchBox's `bif-tui` in the native runner (task W2). Until then `init --answers` is the only form.

title: Command reference
body: Command reference Every command is bxrig NAME ... . This page is generated from docs/reference/cli.json ; the same data answers bxrig help and bxrig help NAME in the terminal. The command contract has the details behind each one. How commands behave Flag What it does --json Print one JSON object instead of text (see below). Every command takes it. --yes Apply a change that installs packages or edits system files. Without it you get the plan and exit code 2. --dry-run Print the plan or the exact commands and exit 0. Nothing is changed. --force Where it exists: replace a file BxRig would otherwise keep because you edited it. Settings that only touch your own config (a theme, the bar, the font) act at once and need no --yes . Exit codes Code Meaning 0 Done, or nothing to do (also --dry-run ). 1 A check came out negative (for example package-status says it is missing). 2 Usage error, or a plan was printed because --yes was not given. 3 Timeout, or the item is not available. 4 A precondition failed: not Arch or CachyOS, a tool or a monitor that is not there, an unknown name. 5 The official (pacman) phase failed. 6 The AUR phase, or the command you asked for, failed. 7 Partial success: some items were done, some failed. 8 Config conflict: a file you edited, or another run is in progress. 9 Internal error. 10 update check : an update is available. JSON { "schema": 1, "command": "dns", "version": "0.11.0", "ok": true, "exit": 0, "dry_run": false, "data": { }, "warnings": [] } data is different for every command; ok is true when exit is 0. Scripts should read exit and data , never the text. All commands Start here : init , refresh , reinstall , wizard , status , doctor , update , version , menu , apps , help Install and remove : install , remove , pkg , catalog , plan , install-plan , optional-plan , profile-plan , profile-install-plan , profile-install , optional-install , profile-list , optional-list , desktop-list , tui-list , web-list , package-status , package-source , dev-plan , prerequisites , apps-doctor , web , toolchain Desktop setup : setup , session , tiling , plasma , keys , runner , default , layout , assets , config Look and feel : theme , appearance , display , power , time , toggle , nightshift , notify System and security : system , security , dns , kernel , ssh , secrets , vpn , cloud , settings , dotfiles , nas , backup , timemachine , java , sdk , mail , tui , bxtimemachine Develop : boxlang , editor , db , containers , vm , ai , skills Everyday tools : screenshot , qr , record , clipboard , emoji , forcequit , window , overview , quicklook , dolphin , dictation , strata , gpu , input , airplay Start here Set up the machine, see where it stands, keep it current. bxrig init {#bxrig-init} The setup wizard: asks the questions, shows a review, then runs the matching commands. bxrig init [--from=FILE] [--fresh | --rerun] | init --answers=FILE [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json] | init --print-answers [--from-system] [--json] | init --export=FILE [--force] Changes the system: needs --yes . Without it you get the plan (exit 2); --dry-run shows it and exits 0. bxrig init bxrig init --answers=answers.json --yes bxrig init --print-answers --from-system --json bxrig refresh {#bxrig-refresh} Put a managed config back to what BxRig ships, with a backup first and without installing anything. bxrig refresh hyprland|noctalia|terminals|shell|nvim|theme|all [--starter] [--force] [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json] bxrig refresh list [--json] Changes the system: needs --yes .
