# Command reference

Every command is `bxrig NAME ...`. This page is generated from `docs/reference/cli.json`; the same data answers `bxrig help` and `bxrig help NAME` in the terminal. The [command contract](/architecture/COMMAND-CONTRACT/index.html) has the details behind each one.

## How commands behave

|    Flag     |                                               What it does                                                |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--json`    | Print one JSON object instead of text (see below). Every command takes it.                                |
| `--yes`     | Apply a change that installs packages or edits system files. Without it you get the plan and exit code 2. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the plan or the exact commands and exit 0. Nothing is changed.                                      |
| `--force`   | Where it exists: replace a file BxRig would otherwise keep because you edited it.                         |

Settings that only touch your own config (a theme, the bar, the font) act at once and need no `--yes`.

### Exit codes

| Code |                                               Meaning                                               |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Done, or nothing to do (also `--dry-run`).                                                          |
| 1    | A check came out negative (for example `package-status` says it is missing).                        |
| 2    | Usage error, or a plan was printed because `--yes` was not given.                                   |
| 3    | Timeout, or the item is not available.                                                              |
| 4    | A precondition failed: not Arch or CachyOS, a tool or a monitor that is not there, an unknown name. |
| 5    | The official (pacman) phase failed.                                                                 |
| 6    | The AUR phase, or the command you asked for, failed.                                                |
| 7    | Partial success: some items were done, some failed.                                                 |
| 8    | Config conflict: a file you edited, or another run is in progress.                                  |
| 9    | Internal error.                                                                                     |
| 10   | `update check`: an update is available.                                                             |

### JSON

```json
{ "schema": 1, "command": "dns", "version": "0.11.0", "ok": true, "exit": 0, "dry_run": false, "data": { }, "warnings": [] }
```

`data` is different for every command; `ok` is true when `exit` is 0. Scripts should read `exit` and `data`, never the text.

## Start here

Set up the machine, see where it stands, keep it current.

### `bxrig init` {#bxrig-init}

The setup wizard: asks the questions, shows a review, then runs the matching commands.

```text
bxrig init [--from=FILE] [--fresh | --rerun] | init --answers=FILE [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json] | init --print-answers [--from-system] [--json] | init --export=FILE [--force]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig init
bxrig init --answers=answers.json --yes
bxrig init --print-answers --from-system --json
```

### `bxrig refresh` {#bxrig-refresh}

Put a managed config back to what BxRig ships, with a backup first and without installing anything.

```text
bxrig refresh hyprland|noctalia|terminals|shell|nvim|theme|all [--starter] [--force] [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
bxrig refresh list [--json]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig refresh list
bxrig refresh terminals --dry-run
bxrig refresh hyprland --yes
bxrig refresh shell --yes --force
```

> A file you edited is kept and reported; --force overwrites it after a backup (see config history and config restore). --starter also rewrites the starter hyprland.lua or Noctalia config.toml, which are yours.

### `bxrig reinstall` {#bxrig-reinstall}

Run the setup wizard again from your saved answers (the same as init --rerun).

```text
bxrig reinstall [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig reinstall
```

> This is the way to install packages again. refresh only puts config files back.

### `bxrig wizard` {#bxrig-wizard}

Wizard pieces for scripts: render the demo screens or a pages file.

```text
bxrig wizard --demo [--out=FILE] | --pages=FILE [--out=FILE] [--answers=FILE]
```

```bash
bxrig wizard --demo
```

### `bxrig status` {#bxrig-status}

What is installed and configured on this machine, compared with what BxRig would do.

```text
bxrig status [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig status
bxrig status --json
```

### `bxrig doctor` {#bxrig-doctor}

Checks the machine (Arch or CachyOS, pacman, sudo, disk) and reports problems.

```text
bxrig doctor [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig doctor
```

### `bxrig update` {#bxrig-update}

Check for a BxRig update, apply it, pick a channel, turn the daily notification on or off.

```text
bxrig update check [--notify] | apply [--yes] | channel [stable|beta] | notifications on|off|status [--json]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig update check
bxrig update apply --yes
bxrig update channel beta
bxrig update notifications on
```

> Exit 10 from `update check` means an update is available.

### `bxrig version` {#bxrig-version}

The BxRig version and build.

```text
bxrig version [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig version
```

### `bxrig menu` {#bxrig-menu}

The control center: every command as a menu on your launcher (Rofi, Walker, Wofi, Fuzzel or Vicinae).

```text
bxrig menu | menu items [--json] | menu search TEXT [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig menu
bxrig menu search 'time zone'
```

> Bind it to a key; the first entry, Search, lists every entry as one flat list.

### `bxrig apps` {#bxrig-apps}

Your installed catalog apps, as a list or a launcher grid.

```text
bxrig apps | apps list [--json]
```

```bash
bxrig apps list
```

### `bxrig help` {#bxrig-help}

This list, or the usage of one command.

```text
bxrig help [COMMAND]
```

```bash
bxrig help

```

## Install and remove

Apps from the catalog, any package from the repositories or the AUR, and the reverse.

### `bxrig install` {#bxrig-install}

Install catalog apps by id (or a whole group or profile).

```text
bxrig install [NAME] [--optional] [--shell=hyprland|plasma|all] [--json] [--yes] [--dry-run]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig install --dry-run
bxrig install --yes
```

> With no name it installs the default set; without --yes it prints the plan and changes nothing.

### `bxrig remove` {#bxrig-remove}

Uninstall catalog apps (their packages or web launchers).

```text
bxrig remove ID_OR_PACKAGE... [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig remove lazygit --yes
```

> Protected packages (the base system, the kernel, bxrig itself) are refused.

### `bxrig pkg` {#bxrig-pkg}

Search, inspect, install and remove any package from the repositories and the AUR.

```text
bxrig pkg search TEXT [--source=all|repo|aur] [--limit=N] | info NAME | installed [--explicit] | install NAME... [--aur] [--yes] [--dry-run] | remove NAME... [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig pkg search ripgrep
bxrig pkg install ripgrep --yes
bxrig pkg remove htop --yes
```

Browse the app catalog.

```text
bxrig catalog list [--group=G] [--category=C] [--tier=default|optional] [--kind=K] [--source=S] [--json] | show ID | groups | check | version
```

```bash
bxrig catalog groups
bxrig catalog list --group=ai --tier=default
bxrig catalog show lazygit
```

```bash
bxrig plan
```

```text
bxrig profile-install NAME [--optional] [--shell=hyprland|plasma|all] [--json] [--yes] [--dry-run]
```

### `bxrig optional-list` {#bxrig-optional-list}

### `bxrig package-status` {#bxrig-package-status}

## Desktop setup

Hyprland with Noctalia, or KDE Plasma beside it: the session, the keys, the defaults.

### `bxrig setup` {#bxrig-setup}

```text

```

Changes the system: needs `--yes`. Without it you get the plan (exit 2); `--dry-run` shows it and exits 0.

```bash
bxrig setup hyprland --yes
bxrig setup terminal --default=ghostty --also=kitty --yes
```

# BxRig

**BxRig** brings an opinionated, beautiful and efficient desktop to Linux, built for developers. It turns a fresh CachyOS or Arch install into a finished developer rig: Hyprland with Noctalia (KDE Plasma stays installed beside it), BoxLang and MatchBox, your apps, your shell, your AI agents, all chosen in one guided setup. It is a single native program written in [BoxLang](https://boxlang.io) and compiled with [MatchBox](https://matchbox.boxlang.io).

**Supported today: CachyOS and Arch Linux. Other distributions (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora) are the direction, not yet supported.**

*This is the documentation for version 1.0.x.*

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL {{ installUrl }} | bash
```

It checks your machine, downloads and verifies the release, installs everything, then starts the setup wizard. See [Getting started](/getting-started/index.html).

## What you get

Hyprland and Noctalia, or Plasma with tiling and a status panel. Mac-style keys, screenshots, notifications, night shift.

The control center: search every setting, install any package, change the look, monitors, power, time zone and DNS.

Your setup, your system and your files, backed up to a NAS or the cloud, and one screen to go back through time.

One terminal for your machine: what needs attention, what runs and how fresh your backups are.

A local inbox for the mail your apps send while you develop. One command, nothing leaves your machine.

A curated catalog of 280 apps and web apps, with one-click Google, Microsoft and Apple suites.

BoxLang, MatchBox, their version managers, VS Code with the extension, and modules from ForgeBox.

Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and more, with keys in your keyring and skills that teach them BxRig.

## How it behaves

* Nothing changes until you say so: every command prints a plan and needs `--yes`.
* Files you edit are kept. BxRig only rewrites files it wrote itself.
* Everything is also a command, with `--json` output, so you can script it.

# The setup wizard

`bxrig init` opens a full-screen form with these pages: **Desktop** , **Look** , **Input** , **Developer** , **Toolchains** , **Containers** , **Apps** , **AI** , **Extras** and **Import**, then a review screen that lists exactly the commands it will run. Nothing runs until you confirm.

## Run it again

On a machine that is already set up the wizard starts from your saved answers plus what it finds on the system, and marks installed options with `✓ installed`.

|         Command          |                    Starts from                    |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `bxrig init`             | your saved answers and what the system has (tune) |
| `bxrig init --rerun`     | your saved answers only                           |
| `bxrig init --fresh`     | the defaults                                      |
| `bxrig init --from FILE` | an answers file from another machine              |

Nothing the machine already has is ever removed. `bxrig status` shows the same scan without opening the wizard.

## Without a terminal

```bash
bxrig init --answers answers.json --yes     # apply an answers file
bxrig init --defaults --yes                  # the wizard's default answers
bxrig init --dry-run                         # show the plan only
bxrig init --export answers.json             # save your answers for another machine
```

Answers are saved in `~/.config/bxrig/answers.json` (mode 600). They never contain secrets.

## Defaults worth knowing

|   Question   |                       Default                       |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Desktop      | Hyprland + Noctalia                                 |
| Workspaces   | 4                                                   |
| Shell        | zsh with the Starship prompt (Catppuccin Powerline) |
| Terminal     | Ghostty                                             |
| File manager | Strata                                              |
| Toolchains   | Java and Rust                                       |
| Containers   | Podman (with `docker` commands mapped to it)        |
| Dictation    | Superwhisper (Voxtype is the alternative)           |
| Updates      | stable channel, daily notification                  |

# Getting started

## What you need

**Supported today: CachyOS and Arch Linux. Other distributions (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora) are the direction, not yet supported.**

* CachyOS or Arch Linux (a system with `pacman`), x86_64.
* A normal user with `sudo`. The installer refuses to run as root.
* A network connection.

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL {{ installUrl }} | bash
```

The installer:

1. checks the machine;
2. downloads the program and the install bundle for your [channel](/guides/updates/index.html) and verifies their signature and SHA-256;
3. installs packages, toolchains (Java 21, `bvm`, `mvm`, BoxLang, MatchBox, Rust) and the core apps;
4. starts the [setup wizard](/guides/wizard/index.html).

Its log is `~/.cache/bxrig/install.log`.

### Without anyone at the keyboard

```bash
curl -fsSL {{ installUrl }} | bash -s -- --yes --answers answers.json
```

`--yes` never asks (it needs passwordless sudo). Without `--answers`, the wizard's default answers are applied. More options: `--channel stable|beta`, `--no-wizard`, `--dry-run`.

## After the install

|         Do this         |              With               |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------|
| See what is set up      | `bxrig status`                  |
| Change your choices     | `bxrig init`                    |
| Open the control center | `Super+Alt+M` or `bxrig menu`   |
| See every shortcut      | `Super+K` or `bxrig keys sheet` |
| Check for updates       | `bxrig update check`            |

New to BoxLang? Run `bxrig boxlang welcome` for a getting-started page, or open [Try BoxLang](https://try.boxlang.io).

# MatchBox parity work: class entry, mappings, Application.bx

Source of truth: BoxLang JVM (`ortus-boxlang/boxlang`, read 2026-11-09 at b8ea0f0) and the BoxLang docs (CLI Scripting, Application.bx). MatchBox today (develop + our PRs) supports none of the three for scripts or native builds.

## 1. Class as entry point (`boxlang Task.bx a b`)

JVM: `BoxRuntime.executeTemplate` sends `.bx`/`.cfc` files to `executeClass`.

1. A request context is created and the Application listener is resolved (section 3).
2. The class is instantiated (its `init` is NOT special here; the constructor runs, pseudo-constructor included).
3. If the instance has a `main` member (`this` scope), run `listener.onRequestStart(templatePath)`. If it returns true, call `main( args )` where `args` is an **array of the raw CLI arguments after the file name** , in order (`["hola", "--many", "options=test"]`). `main` may be an instance or static method; `args = []` default is the convention.
4. Errors: abort -\> `onAbort`; missing include -\> `onMissingTemplate`; any other exception -\> log, then `onError(exception, "")`, rethrown if `onError` is false. Always `onRequestEnd(templatePath)` and flush output.
5. No `main`: error `Class [X] does not have a main method to execute.` (non-zero exit).
6. A path without extension is presumed to be `<path>.bx`. `CLIGetArgs()` and `server.cli.parsed` work inside the class as in scripts.

## 2. Mappings

The only ways to declare them (owner decision, matches the JVM):

* `this.mappings` in `Application.bx`.
* `mappings` in `boxlang.json` (runtime config; the JVM default is `{ "/": "${user-dir}" }`).
* The `bx:application` component, which merges all of its attributes into the application settings (`name`, `mappings`, ...), then recomputes the request config.

Value forms: a string path, or a struct `{ path, external }` (`path` required, `external` default `true`; BoxLang 1.6+). Names are normalized to a leading and trailing slash (`models` and `/models/` are the same). Application mappings are merged over the global ones, application wins.

Class resolution order (`BoxResolver.findFromLocal`): 1) relative to the current template, 2) mappings (a mapping matches when the class path, as a slash path, starts with the mapping name; one candidate per valid extension, `.bx` before `.bxs` as configured), 3) custom component/class paths. Applies to `new`, `import`, `extends`, `implements` and `createObject("class", name)`.

## 3. Application.bx for scripts and classes

Discovery (`ApplicationService.loadDescriptorTemplate`): for an absolute script path, the descriptor is looked up in **the script's directory only** ; for non-absolute (mapped) paths it walks up from the template's directory to its mapping root. Lookup order in a directory: class files `Application.bx` (valid class extensions, then `.cfc`), then templates `Application.<template extension>`. The class is instantiated **without calling `init()`**.

Settings read from `this`: `name`, `mappings`, `datasource`/`defaultDatasource`/`datasources`, `javaSettings`, `classPaths`/`componentPaths`, `customComponentPaths`, `caches`, `schedulers`, `watchers`, `timezone`, `locale`, `runtimeSettings`, security extension lists. A settings change recomputes the request config.

Lifecycle for a script or class run (no web scopes): application defined on first use -\> `onApplicationStart()` once (only if `this.name` is set; false aborts) -\> `onRequestStart(targetPage)` (false aborts) -\> run the script (`template.invoke`; `onRequest` is not used for scripts) or `main(args)` -\> `onRequestEnd()` -\> flush. Errors go to `onError(exception, eventName)`; `abort` to `onAbort(targetPage)`. `onApplicationEnd(applicationScope)` on shutdown. Session hooks never fire in CLI.

## 4. Order of MatchBox work

1. Class entry with `main(args)` (interpreter and native).
2. Mappings: `boxlang.json`/`matchbox.toml` mappings plus `this.mappings` read from `Application.bx`; resolution wired into `new`, `import`, `extends`, `createObject`.
3. Application.bx for scripts and classes, with the lifecycle above.

Native builds resolve classes at compile time, so mapped directories must exist when `matchbox --target native` runs; the Application.bx settings that affect compilation (mappings) are read at build time, and the lifecycle runs inside the binary.

## MatchBox VM fixes (PRs 156 to 160, in the `bxcachy` branch)

Found while building the installer, fixed upstream, and BxRig no longer works around them: `break` in nested for-in loops (#156), a broken pipe on stdout (#157), calling a function stored in `variables` (#158), `switch` with `var` slots and the default jump (#159), and the panic message that was hidden (#160). Behaviour change in #159: a `var` declared in one `case` is not visible in another case.

markdown:
# The desktop

BxRig sets up **Hyprland with Noctalia** as the main desktop. **KDE Plasma** stays installed and gets tiling and a status panel; pick either (or both) at the login screen (`bxrig session set hyprland|plasma`).

## Hyprland and Noctalia

`bxrig setup hyprland` installs the packages one by one and writes the starter configuration once. `~/.config/hypr/hyprland.lua` is yours. BxRig owns `~/.config/hypr/bxrig.lua`, which it regenerates from the [shortcut table](/guides/shortcuts/index.html); never edit that file by hand.

## KDE Plasma

* **Tiling:** `bxrig setup plasma` installs HyprKwin. Layouts: dwindle, master, monocle, scrolling, stage. `bxrig tiling on|off|status|layout NAME`.
* **Panels:** `bxrig plasma panels apply` replaces your panels with a top status panel (launcher, workspace pager, active window, clock, weather, media, system vitals, tray, in rounded islands with Panel Colorizer) and a bottom dock. Your old layout is backed up first: `bxrig plasma panels undo --yes` restores it. From Hyprland it is applied at your next Plasma login.
* **Virtual desktops:** `bxrig plasma desktops 4`.

Look and hardware have their own pages: [Appearance](/guides/appearance/index.html) for the bar, dock, windows and fonts, and [Displays, power and time](/guides/system/index.html) for monitors, laptop power and the time zone. The [control center](/guides/menu/index.html) has all of it as one menu.

## Everyday tools

|          Do          |                    Command                     |              Shortcut              |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Control center       | `bxrig menu`                                   | `Super+Alt+M`                      |
| All apps window      | `bxrig apps`                                   | `Super+Alt+Space`                  |
| Screenshot           | `bxrig screenshot screen\|region\|window`      | `Super+Shift+3` / `4` / `5` (menu) |
| Text from the screen | `bxrig screenshot ocr`                         | in the `5` menu                    |
| QR codes             | `bxrig screenshot qr`, `bxrig qr TEXT`         |                                    |
| Record the screen    | `bxrig record toggle [--region]`               | `Super+Shift+R`                    |
| Clipboard history    | `bxrig clipboard pick`                         | `Super+Shift+V`                    |
| Do Not Disturb       | `bxrig notify dnd toggle`, `notify snooze 30m` | `Super+Alt+N`                      |
| Night shift          | `bxrig nightshift on\|off\|toggle`             | `Super+Alt+Shift+N`                |
| Emoji                | `bxrig emoji`                                  | `Super+Ctrl+E`                     |
| Force quit           | `bxrig forcequit`                              | `Super+Alt+Escape`                 |
| Overview             | `bxrig overview`                               | `Super+Ctrl+Up`                    |
| Minimize / restore   | `bxrig window minimize\|restore`               | `Super+M` / `Super+Shift+M`        |
| Pull-down AI shell   | `bxrig ai shell`                               | ``Super+```                        |

Night shift on Hyprland runs `wlsunset` with your time zone's sunrise and sunset (no network lookup); on Plasma it turns on Plasma's own Night Light.

## Trackpads and Apple devices

`bxrig input gestures --yes` sets up three-finger swipes (workspaces, overview) with `libinput-gestures`. `bxrig input doctor` checks Magic Mouse and Magic Trackpad support (the kernel driver, Bluetooth, the `input` group). For Option-key characters like a Mac, pick the **English (US, Macintosh)** keyboard layout in the wizard. `bxrig airplay on` starts an AirPlay receiver.

## Hot corners

Hot corners are left to you: on Plasma use System Settings → Screen Edges.

markdown:
# Appearance

`bxrig appearance` changes how the shell and the windows look. Each change acts at once, is remembered, and can be shown first with `--dry-run`. For colors, see [Themes](/guides/themes/index.html).

```bash
bxrig appearance status
bxrig appearance bar position bottom      # top, bottom, left, right
bxrig appearance bar style glassy         # opaque, glassy, clear
bxrig appearance bar clock iso            # ten clock formats (time-24h, sunday-12h, date-24h, iso ...)
bxrig appearance bar battery on           # the percentage next to the battery
bxrig appearance dock mode autohide       # always, autohide, off
bxrig appearance windows gaps off         # no gaps and no borders
bxrig appearance windows corners sharp    # theme, rounded, sharp
bxrig appearance windows opacity glassy   # opaque, glassy
bxrig appearance animations off
bxrig appearance layout scrolling         # dwindle, scrolling, floating
bxrig appearance font list
bxrig appearance font install cascadia --yes
bxrig appearance font cascadia            # Noctalia and the terminals follow
bxrig appearance background random        # or: list, set NAME, next
bxrig appearance apply                    # push everything you chose again
```

## Where the changes go

* **Noctalia** (bar, dock, clock, battery, font, corner radius) is changed with `noctalia msg config-set`, so your `config.toml` is not edited. Without Noctalia the choice is saved and `appearance apply` pushes it later.
* **Hyprland** window looks (gaps, corners, opacity, animations, layout) are one generated file, `~/.config/bxrig/theme/look.lua`, loaded by `bxrig.lua`. BxRig reloads Hyprland after a change. Your own `hyprland.lua` is never touched.
* **Fonts** come from seven Nerd Fonts. Changing the font also updates the terminal configs BxRig wrote, but never one you edited (it tells you which).
* **Backgrounds** are read from `~/Pictures/BxRig`, `~/Pictures` and the current theme's folder.

The menu has all of this under Appearance.

markdown:
# Shortcuts and Mac keys

BxRig keeps one shortcut table and renders it for xremap (Cmd-style keys, on both desktops), the Hyprland module and Plasma. Press `Super+K` (or run `bxrig keys sheet`) to see every shortcut in your menu program.

## Cmd-style keys

With Mac keys on, the Super key works like Cmd in apps: `Super+C V X Z A S F T N O P R W L B I U` and `Super+,` send the Ctrl version. In terminals `Super+C/V` copy and paste with `Ctrl+Shift`, `Super+T/N/W/F` become `Ctrl+Shift+T/N/W/F`, and the shell keys (`Ctrl+Z`, `Ctrl+A`...) are left alone. `bxrig keys mac on|off` toggles it.

## Change a shortcut

```bash
bxrig keys show                         # the table
bxrig keys set control-center Super+Alt+C --yes
bxrig keys reset control-center --yes
bxrig keys conflicts                    # clashes with your own hyprland.lua
```

Your changes live in `~/.config/bxrig/shortcuts.json`. Remaps (the Cmd keys) are xremap's and cannot be changed this way.

## The main ones

|            Keys             |                Does                |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `Super+Alt+M`               | Control center                     |
| `Super+Alt+Space`           | All apps                           |
| `Super+K`                   | Shortcut cheat sheet               |
| `Super+Shift+3` / `4` / `5` | Screenshot: screen / region / menu |
| `Super+Shift+R`             | Screen recording                   |
| `Super+Shift+V`             | Clipboard history                  |
| `Super+Ctrl+E`              | Emoji                              |
| `Super+Ctrl+X`              | Dictation on or off (Voxtype)      |
| `Super+Alt+N`               | Do Not Disturb                     |
| `Super+Q`                   | Close window                       |
| `Super+M` / `Super+Shift+M` | Minimize / show minimized          |

markdown:
# The setup wizard

The BxRig setup wizard: a full-screen terminal form written in BoxLang on MatchBox's terminal canvas (`docs/tui.md` in the MatchBox repo). It draws pages given as
JSON and writes the answers as JSON. It runs nothing itself; `bxrig init` starts it and acts on the answers
(COMMAND-CONTRACT.md section 14).

    bxrig wizard --pages=pages.json --out=answers.json [--answers=saved.json]
    bxrig wizard --demo [--out=answers.json]        # built-in pages, to try it

Exit codes: 0 answers written, 130 cancelled (nothing written), 2 usage, 4 unreadable pages or answers file.

## Pages

```json
{ "title": "BxRig", "tagline": "...", "version": "0.12.0",
  "pages": [ { "id": "desktop", "title": "Desktop", "intro": "...",
    "questions": [
      { "type": "choice",  "id": "desktops", "label": "...", "help": "...", "default": "both",
        "options": [ { "value": "hyprland", "label": "Hyprland", "description": "shown under the list when focused", "group": "optional heading" } ] },
      { "type": "multi",   "id": "layouts",  "label": "...", "default": ["us"], "options": [ ... ] },
      { "type": "text",    "id": "git_name", "label": "...", "placeholder": "...", "default": "" },
      { "type": "number",  "id": "workspaces", "label": "...", "min": 1, "max": 10, "default": 2 },
      { "type": "confirm", "id": "natural_scroll", "label": "...", "default": false },
      { "type": "info",    "label": "...", "help": "..." } ] } ] }
```

Any question may carry `"when": { "id": "other_question", "in": ["a", "b"] }` (or `"equals": "a"`): it is shown only while that answer matches, and a hidden question is left out of the review and the answers file.

A whole page may carry `when` too: it is then skipped by Next and Back and left out of the sidebar, the step count, the review and the result. `bxrig init` adds one page per catalog group after the Apps page this way (see `AppPages`), shown only for "Customize".

Answers are a flat JSON object keyed by question id: a string (choice, text), an array of strings (multi), a number, or a bool.

## Keys and mouse

Up/Down (or j/k) move, Space selects or toggles, Enter finishes the question and moves on, Left/Right change a number,
Tab/PageDown next page, Esc/Shift-Tab/PageUp previous page, Ctrl-C cancels. Clicks select options and jump to visited steps.
Text fields take typing directly (Backspace deletes, Ctrl-U clears).

## Look

Catppuccin Frappe neutrals with the Ortus brand gradient (cyan `#00DBFF` to green `#00FF78`), true colour, a fade-in between
screens and a soft shimmer. The splash uses the official BoxLang icon as half-block pixel art (`assets/wizard/art-*.txt`, embedded by `bootstrap/gen-wizard.sh` into `src/bxrig/WizardData.bx`). Every screen shows "Powered by BoxLang / [www.boxlang.io](http://www.boxlang.io)". It needs a 76x24 terminal; larger is nicer.

## Code

|    Class     |                                             Does                                             |
|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `WizardApp`  | State and key handling, no drawing (unit tested).                                            |
| `WizardView` | Draws a frame on the canvas and records click regions; testable with `tui.render_to_string`. |
| `Wizard`     | The run loop: events in, frames out.                                                         |
| `WizardData` | Generated: demo pages and splash art.                                                        |

## Developing

Needs MatchBox built with `bif-tui`.

    (cd src && matchbox ../tests/wizard_app_test.bxs)    # logic
    (cd src && matchbox ../tests/wizard_view_test.bxs)   # what each screen shows
    bash tests/wizard-test.sh BXRIG_NATIVE             # end to end in a pseudo-terminal
    python3 tools/record-wizard.py --bin BXRIG_NATIVE --out /tmp/rec   # mp4 and gif (needs Pillow, pyte, ffmpeg)

title: Themes
body: Themes BxRig ships 15 color themes in the Omarchy theme format: five of ours and ten taken from Omarchy. bxrig theme list # all themes, the current one marked bxrig theme set tokyo-night # apply one now bxrig theme next # or random bxrig theme mode auto # theme, dark, light or auto bxrig theme status Setting a theme acts at once. --dry-run shows what would be written without changing anything. What changes Where How Noctalia (bar, launcher, panels, notifications) a generated palette and the light or dark mode Ghostty, kitty, alacritty, foot generated files that the starter configs include btop a generated theme file Hyprland window borders the accent color, read by the managed bxrig.lua Neovim (LazyVim setup) the matching colorscheme, applied live without a restart KDE Plasma switches between Breeze Light and Breeze Dark GTK 3 and 4 apps ~/.config/gtk-4.0/gtk.css and gtk-3.0/gtk.css (libadwaita colors; adw-gtk3 for GTK 3), plus the dark or light preference through gsettings Qt apps qt6ct and qt5ct color schemes (set the style to qt6ct in your environment) tmux, fzf theme/tmux.conf and theme/fzf.sh , with a one-line hint to source them rofi, fuzzel, wofi a rofi theme (and a config.rasi stub when you have none), fuzzel.ini , wofi style.css Wallpaper a BxRig theme brings one of our wallpapers; use --keep-wallpaper to skip it VS Code is opt-in: bxrig theme vscode shows a plan, --yes merges the colors into workbench.colorCustomizations of Code, Code - OSS, VSCodium or Cursor (a backup is kept; a settings file with comments is left alone). Not themed: the Starship prompt, browsers and icons. Your own config files are never edited. Terminal configs you wrote yourself need one include line, which bxrig theme set prints. Bar, dock, windows, fonts and backgrounds are in Appearance . The themes BxRig, BxRig Light, BxRig Midnight, BxRig Cyan and BxRig Forest are ours. From Omarchy: catppuccin, catppuccin-latte, tokyo-night, gruvbox, nord, rose-pine, kanagawa, everforest, matte-black and flexoki-light (MIT, credited in themes/NOTICE.md ). More themes, and your own bxrig theme install https://github.com/someone/omarchy-name-theme installs an Omarchy-style theme repository (https only). Themes you already have in ~/.config/omarchy/themes are found automatically. A theme is a folder with colors.toml , an optional neovim.lua and an optional backgrounds/ folder: bxrig theme import ~/my-theme --name=mine bxrig theme remove mine Both colors.toml formats are understood: the named colors of current Omarchy and the older color0 to color15 list. Neovim bxrig editor lazyvim --yes installs the LazyVim starter plus the BxRig layer: transparent background, BoxLang syntax highlighting ( vim-boxlang ), no news popups, the neo-tree extra, and live theme following. An existing ~/.config/nvim is never touched. To add only BoxLang syntax to a LazyVim config you already have: bxrig editor boxlang --yes . The BoxLang prompt segment The starter Starship prompt shows your BoxLang version, like Java, in folders with .bx , .bxs , .bxm , .cfc , .cfm or .cfs files, box.json or Application.bx . The starter file is written once, so an existing prompt keeps what you have; bxrig config diff starship shows what is new.
markdown:
# Themes

BxRig ships 15 color themes in the Omarchy theme format: five of ours and ten taken from Omarchy.

```bash
bxrig theme list                  # all themes, the current one marked
bxrig theme set tokyo-night       # apply one now
bxrig theme next                  # or random
bxrig theme mode auto             # theme, dark, light or auto
bxrig theme status
```

Setting a theme acts at once. `--dry-run` shows what would be written without changing anything.

## What changes

|                      Where                      |                                                                      How                                                                       |
|-------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Noctalia (bar, launcher, panels, notifications) | a generated palette and the light or dark mode                                                                                                 |
| Ghostty, kitty, alacritty, foot                 | generated files that the starter configs include                                                                                               |
| btop                                            | a generated theme file                                                                                                                         |
| Hyprland window borders                         | the accent color, read by the managed `bxrig.lua`                                                                                              |
| Neovim (LazyVim setup)                          | the matching colorscheme, applied live without a restart                                                                                       |
| KDE Plasma                                      | switches between Breeze Light and Breeze Dark                                                                                                  |
| GTK 3 and 4 apps                                | `~/.config/gtk-4.0/gtk.css` and `gtk-3.0/gtk.css` (libadwaita colors; adw-gtk3 for GTK 3), plus the dark or light preference through gsettings |
| Qt apps                                         | qt6ct and qt5ct color schemes (set the style to qt6ct in your environment)                                                                     |
| tmux, fzf                                       | `theme/tmux.conf` and `theme/fzf.sh`, with a one-line hint to source them                                                                      |
| rofi, fuzzel, wofi                              | a rofi theme (and a `config.rasi` stub when you have none), `fuzzel.ini`, wofi `style.css`                                                     |
| Wallpaper                                       | a BxRig theme brings one of our wallpapers; use `--keep-wallpaper` to skip it                                                                  |

VS Code is opt-in: `bxrig theme vscode` shows a plan, `--yes` merges the colors into `workbench.colorCustomizations` of Code, Code - OSS, VSCodium or Cursor (a backup is kept; a settings file with comments is left alone). Not themed: the Starship prompt, browsers and icons. Your own config files are never edited. Terminal configs you wrote yourself need one include line, which `bxrig theme set` prints.

Bar, dock, windows, fonts and backgrounds are in [Appearance](/guides/appearance/index.html).

## The themes

BxRig, BxRig Light, BxRig Midnight, BxRig Cyan and BxRig Forest are ours. From Omarchy: catppuccin, catppuccin-latte, tokyo-night, gruvbox, nord, rose-pine, kanagawa, everforest, matte-black and flexoki-light (MIT, credited in `themes/NOTICE.md`).

## More themes, and your own

`bxrig theme install https://github.com/someone/omarchy-name-theme` installs an Omarchy-style theme repository (https only). Themes you already have in `~/.config/omarchy/themes` are found automatically. A theme is a folder with `colors.toml`, an optional `neovim.lua` and an optional `backgrounds/` folder:

```bash
bxrig theme import ~/my-theme --name=mine
bxrig theme remove mine
```

Both `colors.toml` formats are understood: the named colors of current Omarchy and the older `color0` to `color15` list.

## Neovim

`bxrig editor lazyvim --yes` installs the LazyVim starter plus the BxRig layer: transparent background, BoxLang syntax highlighting ([vim-boxlang](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/vim-boxlang)), no news popups, the neo-tree extra, and live theme following. An existing `~/.config/nvim` is never touched. To add only BoxLang syntax to a LazyVim config you already have: `bxrig editor boxlang --yes`.

## The BoxLang prompt segment

The starter Starship prompt shows your BoxLang version, like Java, in folders with `.bx`, `.bxs`, `.bxm`, `.cfc`, `.cfm` or `.cfs` files, `box.json` or `Application.bx`. The starter file is written once, so an existing prompt keeps what you have; `bxrig config diff starship` shows what is new.

# Apps and web apps

## The catalog

BxRig knows about 280 apps and web apps in groups (development, terminal, AI, infrastructure, network, system, desktop, everyday, web apps, media, gaming). Each is **default** (installed by the wizard's Basic mode) or **optional** . Sources: official packages first (`pacman`), then the AUR (`yay`), Omarchy's packages, vendor installers and web apps.

```bash
bxrig catalog list --group media
bxrig catalog show strata
bxrig install vlc heidisql --yes
bxrig profile-install jvm --yes        # a ready-made set
```

In the wizard, **Basic** installs the recommended set; **Customize** lets you tick apps per category. Some entries only apply to one desktop (they say so).

## Web apps

A web app is a frameless window with its own launcher entry.

```bash
bxrig web add Notion https://notion.so --yes
bxrig web list
bxrig web install google --yes         # Docs, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube...
bxrig web install microsoft --yes      # Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive
bxrig web install apple --yes          # iCloud, Pages, Numbers, Keynote, Apple Music, Apple TV
```

The same three are in the wizard (Apps page) and the control center (Web apps).

## Defaults

```bash
bxrig default show
bxrig default browser brave --yes
bxrig default terminal ghostty --yes
bxrig default filemanager strata --yes
```

## Files and sharing

The default file manager is **Strata** ; Dolphin is the alternative (`bxrig dolphin doctor` checks it works outside Plasma). `bxrig strata integrations` adds LocalSend and KDE Connect to Strata's *Send to* menu. `bxrig quicklook PATH` previews a file with Kiview.

## More

|           Area           |                                                  Command                                                  |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dictation                | `bxrig dictation setup superwhisper\|voxtype --yes`                                                       |
| Databases                | `bxrig db list\|start ENGINE\|stop\|status\|logs` (Podman first; HeidiSQL and DBeaver are in the catalog) |
| Cloud storage as folders | `bxrig cloud remotes\|configure\|mount NAME\|status` (RClone Browser is the GUI)                          |
| VPN                      | `bxrig vpn nordvpn setup`                                                                                 |
| Containers               | `bxrig containers doctor\|socket enable\|docker-compat`                                                   |
| Editor                   | `bxrig editor lazyvim`                                                                                    |
| GPU drivers              | `bxrig gpu doctor`                                                                                        |

markdown:
# Displays, power and time

## Displays

```bash
bxrig display list
bxrig display scale DP-2 1.5          # auto or 0.5 to 4
bxrig display rotate DP-2 90
bxrig display mode DP-2 2560x1440@144
bxrig display position DP-2 2880x0
bxrig display mirror on               # the laptop panel on every external monitor
bxrig display laptop off              # refused when no other monitor would be on
bxrig display brightness up           # down, or set 40
bxrig display apply                   # push what is saved again
```

On Hyprland the settings are one generated file, `~/.config/bxrig/theme/monitors.lua`, loaded after your own `hyprland.lua`, and Hyprland reloads. On Plasma they go through `kscreen-doctor`.

## Laptop power

CachyOS does not ship laptop power tools, so BxRig adds them.

```bash
bxrig power status
bxrig power setup --yes               # power-profiles-daemon and upower; nothing happens on a desktop
bxrig power profile saver             # performance, balanced, saver
bxrig power lid lock --yes            # suspend, lock or ignore when the lid closes
bxrig power doctor                    # daemons, the lid, zram, swap for hibernation
```

The lid setting is a logind drop-in and applies from the next login. Hibernation is not configured for you; `doctor` tells you whether your swap is big enough.

## Time zone and travel

```bash
bxrig time status
bxrig time zone Europe/Madrid --yes   # set it (bxrig time zone --list shows them all)
bxrig time sync --yes                 # after you land: set the zone from your IP address
bxrig time auto on --yes              # or follow your location by itself
bxrig time ntp on --yes
```

`time auto on` installs GeoClue and `automatic-timezoned`, writes the service and the GeoClue settings it needs, and enables it. **GeoClue looks your location up online (the Wi-Fi networks around you or your IP address)** , so the plan says so before you agree. `time auto off` removes everything it wrote. If the zone does not follow you, read `journalctl -u automatic-timezoned`.

## DNS, kernels and stay awake

```bash
bxrig dns                              # the servers in use
bxrig dns cloudflare --yes             # google, quad9, custom 9.9.9.10, dhcp
bxrig kernel list
bxrig kernel install linux-cachyos-lts --yes
bxrig toggle stay-awake                # keep the screen from idling (Noctalia)
```

`dns` changes the active NetworkManager connections. `kernel` installs or removes kernel packages with their headers; it never edits the bootloader, never removes the running or the last kernel, and you pick the kernel in the boot menu. Stay awake needs Noctalia (Hyprland); on Plasma use System Settings.

markdown:
# Virtual machines

`bxrig vm` runs full desktops in containers: Windows (the dockur/windows image) and Linux desktops (LinuxServer's webtop, a desktop in your browser). They use Podman, or Docker if you chose it with `bxrig db engine docker`.

```bash
bxrig vm doctor                          # is this machine ready? (KVM, groups, GPU, disk)
bxrig vm create linux dev                # a Ubuntu XFCE desktop called dev
bxrig vm create linux arch --tag=arch-kde --gpu=auto
bxrig vm create windows                  # asks which Windows
bxrig vm list                            # all of them: state, ports, disk used
bxrig vm open dev                        # starts it if needed and opens it
```

`create` shows a plan first; add `--yes` to do it. `--dry-run` never changes anything.

## Linux desktops

`bxrig vm versions linux` lists the tags: Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and Arch with XFCE, KDE Plasma, MATE or i3 (plus LXQt on Ubuntu), and a small Alpine. The default is `ubuntu-xfce`. Make as many as you want; each gets its own port, data folder and password.

`vm open NAME` opens `https://127.0.0.1:PORT/` in your browser. The certificate is self-signed, so accept it once. The user is `bxrig`; show the password with `bxrig vm info NAME --show-password`.

**GPU** (optional): `--gpu=intel` or `--gpu=amd` passes `/dev/dri` in. `--gpu=nvidia` is supported too; it needs the NVIDIA driver 580 or newer and the NVIDIA container toolkit, and it is not available on the Alpine tags. `--gpu=auto` uses `/dev/dri` when the machine has it. `vm doctor` shows what your machine has.

## Windows

You pick the version when you create it:

|            Choice             |    Size     |                         Note                          |
|-------------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `11` Windows 11 Pro           | 7.9 GB      | the usual choice                                      |
| `11l` Windows 11 LTSC         | 4.7 GB      | long-term servicing edition, fewer bundled apps       |
| `11e` Windows 11 Enterprise   | 6.6 GB      | business edition                                      |
| `10` Windows 10 Pro           | 5.7 GB      | older, for legacy needs                               |
| `10l` Windows 10 LTSC         | 4.6 GB      | long-term servicing edition                           |
| `tiny11` Tiny11               | 5.3 GB      | **unofficial** stripped-down build from the community |
| `core11` Tiny11 Core          | 3.0 GB      | **unofficial**, the most stripped-down                |
| `tiny10` Tiny10               | 3.6 GB      | **unofficial** stripped-down Windows 10               |
| `2025`, `2022` Windows Server | 7.6, 6.0 GB | server editions                                       |

`bxrig vm versions windows` shows all 25 (down to Windows 95 and ReactOS). In a script, pass `--version=VALUE`.

Windows installs itself the first time it starts: it downloads the ISO inside the container (3 to 8 GB) and takes a while. Watch it with `bxrig vm open NAME --web`. When it is ready, `bxrig vm open NAME` opens it with FreeRDP, with the clipboard shared and the window resizable. **You need your own Windows license.** The install uses generic trial keys that do not activate Windows.

Windows needs `/dev/kvm`: turn on virtualization in the firmware and put yourself in the `kvm` group. `vm doctor` tells you what is missing. Defaults: half your RAM (4 to 8 GB), half your cores, a 64 GB disk. Change them with `--ram`, `--cpus` and `--disk`.

## Where everything is

|           What            |                                                    Where                                                     |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Disk and files of each VM | `~/.local/share/bxrig/vms/NAME` (`storage` for Windows, `config` for Linux)                                  |
| The VM's record           | `~/.config/bxrig/vms/NAME.json`                                                                              |
| Its password              | your keyring, as `BXRIG_VM_NAME_PASSWORD` (see `bxrig secrets`)                                              |
| Shared folder             | `~/Windows` (drive Z: in Windows) or `~/Shared` (inside the Linux desktop); `--share=PATH` or `--share=none` |
| App menu entry            | `~/.local/share/applications/bxrig-vm-NAME.desktop`                                                          |
| The container images      | in Podman or Docker (`podman image ls`)                                                                      |

`bxrig vm size` shows how much disk each VM uses. Everything listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

## Stop, remove

```bash
bxrig vm stop dev
bxrig vm remove dev            # the container, its data, password and menu entry (it asks first)
bxrig vm remove dev --keep-data
```

Your shared folder is never deleted.

markdown:
# AI agents and skills

## Agents

BxRig installs and launches coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode) and orchestrators.

```bash
bxrig ai list
bxrig ai default claude-code --yes
bxrig ai launch                   # the default agent, with its keys loaded
bxrig ai shell                    # a pull-down terminal (Super+`)
bxrig ai session start            # a persistent tmux session
```

## API keys

Keys are stored in your desktop keyring (BxRig installs one if you have none), never in files or shell history.

```bash
bxrig secrets set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY     # typed hidden
bxrig secrets list
bxrig secrets run ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -- some-command
```

Each key is marked as an AI key or another kind, and agents declare which providers they accept (OpenCode can use several). Exporting keys globally is opt-in. Move keys between machines with `bxrig secrets export` (encrypted with age).

## Local models

`bxrig ai models list|ps|pull MODEL|rm|enable` drives Ollama. `bxrig gpu doctor` shows what your GPU needs (`ollama-cuda` or `ollama-rocm`).

## Skills for every agent

**Skills** are small `SKILL.md` files that teach an agent how to do one thing well. BxRig stores them once in `~/.agents/skills` and links each one into the skills folder of every agent you have (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode). A folder of your own with the same name is never replaced.

```bash
bxrig skills install bxrig boxlang matchbox --yes
bxrig skills status
bxrig skills search matchbox            # the skills.boxlang.io hub
bxrig skills install ortus-boxlang/skills/boxlang-developer~language-fundamentals --yes
bxrig skills update --yes
```

|    Name    |                         What it is                         |
|------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `bxrig`    | Five skills about BxRig itself, shipped inside the program |
| `boxlang`  | BoxLang language fundamentals, from the hub                |
| `matchbox` | The MatchBox runtime, from the hub                         |

The hub ([skills.boxlang.io](https://skills.boxlang.io)) audits every skill. A skill that failed its audit is refused. Skills are optional in the wizard (AI page).

title: Backups and BxTimeMachine
body: Backups and BxTimeMachine BxRig protects three different things, and you can use any of them: Layer What it keeps Tool My BxRig setup Your settings, config files and package list, a small snapshot you can restore in one command BxRig itself The whole system Snapshots of the system before and after every update snapper on Btrfs, Timeshift on other filesystems My files Projects, Documents and your SSH config, encrypted restic, to a NAS, a disk or the cloud Everything shows a plan first and needs --yes . The setup wizard has a NAS page, a Remote backups page and a Backups page, in that order. BxTimeMachine bxrig timemachine # every backup on one timeline bxrig timemachine --local # skip the network places so it opens at once bxrig timemachine --demo # made-up data, nothing runs Places are rows (system, config, each place your files go to, plain NAS copies) and time runs left to right, newest on the right. Points are coloured by how old they are (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). The backup you choose is a card with older ones stacked behind it. Open one to browse its files, filter them, restore, export or send it to another place. Every change shows its plan first and runs only when you press y . Press ? for the keys. My BxRig setup bxrig backup config now bxrig backup config list bxrig backup config diff 20261113T153000 bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --dry-run bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --only=.config/hypr --yes A snapshot is taken by itself before update apply , system update , init , reinstall and refresh (turn it off with backup config auto off ). Restoring takes a safety snapshot of the present first. Secrets and SSH keys are never in a snapshot unless you add --with-secrets , which stores your secrets export, encrypted with a passphrase you type. backup export config ID --to=FILE writes a snapshot as one file to carry to another machine. The whole system bxrig backup snapshots setup --yes # snapper, 5 hourly, 7 daily, 2 weekly, 1 monthly; one before and after every pacman update bxrig backup snapshots list bxrig backup snapshots restore 12 /home/me/projects/app --dry-run There is no automatic whole-system rollback: how to roll back a Btrfs root depends on how your subvolumes are laid out. Boot the snapshot from the boot menu and follow the Arch wiki's snapper page, or restore folders with restore . My files A place is where a restic repository lives. Add one, create it, back up, and schedule it: bxrig backup data target add spaces --type=s3 --endpoint=https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com --bucket=mybackups --ask-keys bxrig backup data init spaces --yes bxrig backup data run --all --yes bxrig backup data schedule daily --yes Place types: local (a disk or folder), a NAS (see below), sftp , rest , s3 (AWS, DigitalOcean Spaces, Wasabi, MinIO), b2 (Backblaze), azure , gs (Google Cloud Storage) and rclone (FTP, WebDAV and anything rclone speaks, set up with bxrig cloud configure ). Access keys are typed hidden and go to your keyring; the repository password is made for you and kept there too, so keep a copy ( bxrig secrets get BXRIG_BACKUP_SPACES_PASSWORD --show ). Losing it loses the backups. The schedule is a user timer: it skips on battery power, catches up after the computer was off, and tells you when a backup fails. backup data restore ID --to=DIR restores into a folder you name, never over your files by itself. backup send ID --from=PLACE --to=PLACE copies a snapshot to a second place (a NAS and the cloud, for a 3-2-1 setup), and backup export data ID --to=FILE.zip writes one as an archive. Your config snapshots travel with your files, so any place protects them too. NAS See Your NAS for adding a Synology or any SMB or NFS share and mounting it by itself.
markdown:
# Backups and BxTimeMachine

BxRig protects three different things, and you can use any of them:

|        Layer         |                                         What it keeps                                         |                       Tool                       |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **My BxRig setup**   | Your settings, config files and package list, a small snapshot you can restore in one command | BxRig itself                                     |
| **The whole system** | Snapshots of the system before and after every update                                         | snapper on Btrfs, Timeshift on other filesystems |
| **My files**         | Projects, Documents and your SSH config, encrypted                                            | restic, to a NAS, a disk or the cloud            |

Everything shows a plan first and needs `--yes`. The setup wizard has a **NAS** page, a **Remote backups** page and a **Backups** page, in that order.

## BxTimeMachine

```bash
bxrig timemachine          # every backup on one timeline
bxrig timemachine --local  # skip the network places so it opens at once
bxrig timemachine --demo   # made-up data, nothing runs
```

Places are rows (system, config, each place your files go to, plain NAS copies) and time runs left to right, newest on the right. Points are coloured by how old they are (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). The backup you choose is a card with older ones stacked behind it. Open one to browse its files, filter them, restore, export or send it to another place. Every change shows its plan first and runs only when you press `y`. Press `?` for the keys.

## My BxRig setup

```bash
bxrig backup config now
bxrig backup config list
bxrig backup config diff 20261113T153000
bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --dry-run
bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --only=.config/hypr --yes
```

A snapshot is taken by itself before `update apply`, `system update`, `init`, `reinstall` and `refresh` (turn it off with `backup config auto off`). Restoring takes a safety snapshot of the present first. Secrets and SSH keys are never in a snapshot unless you add `--with-secrets`, which stores your secrets export, encrypted with a passphrase you type. `backup export config ID --to=FILE` writes a snapshot as one file to carry to another machine.

## The whole system

```bash
bxrig backup snapshots setup --yes     # snapper, 5 hourly, 7 daily, 2 weekly, 1 monthly; one before and after every pacman update
bxrig backup snapshots list
bxrig backup snapshots restore 12 /home/me/projects/app --dry-run
```

There is no automatic whole-system rollback: how to roll back a Btrfs root depends on how your subvolumes are laid out. Boot the snapshot from the boot menu and follow the Arch wiki's snapper page, or restore folders with `restore`.

## My files

A **place** is where a restic repository lives. Add one, create it, back up, and schedule it:

```bash
bxrig backup data target add spaces --type=s3 --endpoint=https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com --bucket=mybackups --ask-keys
bxrig backup data init spaces --yes
bxrig backup data run --all --yes
bxrig backup data schedule daily --yes
```

Place types: `local` (a disk or folder), a NAS (see below), `sftp`, `rest`, `s3` (AWS, DigitalOcean Spaces, Wasabi, MinIO), `b2` (Backblaze), `azure`, `gs` (Google Cloud Storage) and `rclone` (FTP, WebDAV and anything rclone speaks, set up with `bxrig cloud configure`). Access keys are typed hidden and go to your keyring; the repository password is made for you and kept there too, so keep a copy (`bxrig secrets get BXRIG_BACKUP_SPACES_PASSWORD --show`). Losing it loses the backups.

The schedule is a user timer: it skips on battery power, catches up after the computer was off, and tells you when a backup fails. `backup data restore ID --to=DIR` restores into a folder you name, never over your files by itself. `backup send ID --from=PLACE --to=PLACE` copies a snapshot to a second place (a NAS and the cloud, for a 3-2-1 setup), and `backup export data ID --to=FILE.zip` writes one as an archive. Your config snapshots travel with your files, so any place protects them too.

## NAS

See [Your NAS](/guides/nas/index.html) for adding a Synology or any SMB or NFS share and mounting it by itself.

The SMB version is negotiated: the highest one the NAS and your kernel both support. Give --vers=3.1.1 to choose. Automatic mounts are systemd .mount and .automount units: the share mounts the first time something opens it and lets go after ten idle minutes, so a sleeping NAS never blocks your login. nas sync NAME SRC --to=SHARE/PATH is a plain rsync mirror (photos, media). markdown:
# Your NAS

`bxrig nas` keeps every NAS you use: its address, the share, how to reach it, and the mount.

```bash
bxrig nas setup --yes                   # cifs-utils, nfs-utils, smbclient, avahi, rsync
bxrig nas discover                      # find NAS boxes on the network
bxrig nas add synology --host=ds920.local --user=luis --ask-password
bxrig nas shares synology
bxrig nas mount synology backups --yes  # ~/NAS/synology/backups
bxrig nas auto on synology backups --yes
bxrig nas test synology
bxrig nas use synology backups          # a place for bxrig backup data
```

* **Passwords** are typed hidden and kept in your keyring. SMB mounts are made by root (also at boot), so the password is also kept in `/etc/bxrig/nas/NAME.cred`, readable by root only; the plan tells you before it writes it. NFS needs no password.
* **The SMB version** is negotiated: the highest one the NAS and your kernel both support. Give `--vers=3.1.1` to choose.
* **Automatic mounts** are systemd `.mount` and `.automount` units: the share mounts the first time something opens it and lets go after ten idle minutes, so a sleeping NAS never blocks your login.
* **`nas sync NAME SRC --to=SHARE/PATH`** is a plain `rsync` mirror (photos, media). Nothing on the NAS is deleted unless you add `--delete`.
* **`nas test`** checks that the NAS answers, that your password works, that the share is mounted and writable, and how much space is free.

Not yet tried on a real Synology: share permissions in DSM, SMB signing and NFS export options. If a mount fails, `bxrig nas test NAME` says which step.

markdown:
# BoxLang and MatchBox

The installer puts in Java 21, **bvm** (BoxLang Version Manager), **mvm** (MatchBox Version Manager), BoxLang and MatchBox. `bxrig boxlang` sits on top of them.

```bash
bxrig boxlang status
bxrig boxlang use latest              # bvm: install if missing, then use
bxrig boxlang use snapshot
bxrig boxlang matchbox use latest     # mvm
bxrig boxlang modules list            # the live ForgeBox list
bxrig boxlang modules search ai
bxrig boxlang modules install bx-ai bx-sites
bxrig boxlang modules update
bxrig boxlang vscode                  # the BoxLang extension and developer pack
bxrig boxlang links                   # docs and sites
bxrig boxlang welcome                 # a getting-started page
```

Modules come from [ForgeBox](https://forgebox.io) and install with `bx-module`. VS Code is a default app; the wizard offers to add the BoxLang extension (`ortus-solutions.vscode-boxlang`) and the developer pack.

## Compile to a native binary

```bash
matchbox script.bxs
```

[MatchBox](https://matchbox.boxlang.io) compiles BoxLang to bytecode on a Rust runtime and can build standalone native binaries. BxRig itself is built this way.

## Links

[Try BoxLang](https://try.boxlang.io) · [Docs](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com) · [BoxLang AI](https://ai.boxlang.io) · [BoxLang Agents](https://bxagents.ai) · [BoxLang Sites](https://bxsites.io) · [ForgeBox](https://forgebox.io) · [Skills](https://skills.boxlang.io)

markdown:
# Updates and channels

## Channels

| Channel  |                        What it is                         |
|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `stable` | Tagged releases                                           |
| `beta`   | The bleeding edge: a build of every push to `development` |

```bash
bxrig update channel            # show
bxrig update channel beta       # switch
```

Both are also in the control center (Settings → Updates).

## Update BxRig

```bash
bxrig update check              # exit 10 means an update is available
bxrig update apply --yes        # download, verify, replace atomically
```

The release information is signed (Ed25519) and the binary's SHA-256 is checked against it; a bad signature or checksum changes nothing.

## Get told about updates

```bash
bxrig update notifications on     # a daily user timer shows a desktop notification
bxrig update notifications off
```

The notification covers BxRig and pending system packages.

## Update the system

```bash
bxrig system update --yes       # snapshot first (snapper or timeshift), then pacman -Syu and yay -Sua
```

## Agent skills

`bxrig skills update --yes` refreshes the skills BxRig installed.

markdown:
# Move to another machine

```bash
bxrig settings export my-settings.tar.gz
bxrig settings import my-settings.tar.gz --yes
```

Export bundles `~/.config/bxrig` (answers, shortcuts, runner and update settings) **without secrets, backups or state** . Import backs up each existing file as `NAME.bak-STAMP` first and refuses archives with paths outside `bxrig/`.

Keys travel separately and encrypted: `bxrig secrets export` and `bxrig secrets import`.

To set up a new machine without touching the old one, export only the wizard answers: `bxrig init --export answers.json`, then on the new machine `bxrig init --from answers.json`, or run unattended with `--answers answers.json --yes`.

title: Security
body: Security Releases are signed. CI signs each channel's version-latest.properties and install.sh with an Ed25519 key. The public key is built into the program and into the published installer. The installer and bxrig update verify the signature and the SHA-256 of every file they download; any mismatch stops before anything changes. The first curl | bash trusts the script it downloads (TLS and the bucket). For a stricter first install, download install.sh and install.sh.sig and check the signature yourself with keys/release.pub . Nothing runs without a plan. Commands that change the system print a plan and need --yes . Your files are yours. BxRig keeps a config you changed and only rewrites files it wrote; every write is atomic, backed up and journaled. Secrets live in the desktop keyring (or a private file fallback), are typed hidden, and never appear in answers files, logs or shell history. Skills from the hub are audited; one that failed its audit is refused. Fingerprint, security key, SSH and passwordless sudo bxrig security can turn on a fingerprint or a security key for sudo , the SSH server and passwordless sudo. These touch PAM and sudoers, so they are guarded. bxrig security status bxrig security fingerprint on --dry-run # prints the exact PAM line first bxrig security fingerprint on --yes bxrig security fingerprint enroll --yes bxrig security fido2 register --yes # touch the key; `fido2 on` refuses until one is registered bxrig security fido2 on --yes bxrig security ssh-server on --yes bxrig security passwordless-sudo on --yes Only /etc/pam.d/sudo is changed , never the login, the login screen or the lock screen. The line is auth sufficient , so your password still works when the reader or key is missing. The first time, the original is kept as /etc/pam.d/sudo.bxrig-backup ; off removes exactly the line BxRig added. sudoers is checked with visudo -cf before the file is installed, so a mistake cannot lock sudo out. Passwordless sudo means any program running as you gets root without a password. Use it only on a machine where you accept that. Keep a root terminal open the first time you try PAM changes. They have not been tried on a real reader or key yet.
markdown:
# Security

* **Releases are signed.** CI signs each channel's `version-latest.properties` and `install.sh` with an Ed25519 key. The public key is built into the program and into the published installer. The installer and `bxrig update` verify the signature and the SHA-256 of every file they download; any mismatch stops before anything changes.
* **The first `curl | bash`** trusts the script it downloads (TLS and the bucket). For a stricter first install, download `install.sh` and `install.sh.sig` and check the signature yourself with `keys/release.pub`.
* **Nothing runs without a plan.** Commands that change the system print a plan and need `--yes`.
* **Your files are yours.** BxRig keeps a config you changed and only rewrites files it wrote; every write is atomic, backed up and journaled.
* **Secrets** live in the desktop keyring (or a private file fallback), are typed hidden, and never appear in answers files, logs or shell history.
* **Skills** from the hub are audited; one that failed its audit is refused.

## Fingerprint, security key, SSH and passwordless sudo

`bxrig security` can turn on a fingerprint or a security key for `sudo`, the SSH server and passwordless sudo. These touch PAM and sudoers, so they are guarded.

```bash
bxrig security status
bxrig security fingerprint on --dry-run   # prints the exact PAM line first
bxrig security fingerprint on --yes
bxrig security fingerprint enroll --yes
bxrig security fido2 register --yes       # touch the key; `fido2 on` refuses until one is registered
bxrig security fido2 on --yes
bxrig security ssh-server on --yes
bxrig security passwordless-sudo on --yes
```

* **Only `/etc/pam.d/sudo` is changed** , never the login, the login screen or the lock screen. The line is `auth sufficient`, so your password still works when the reader or key is missing. The first time, the original is kept as `/etc/pam.d/sudo.bxrig-backup`; `off` removes exactly the line BxRig added.
* **sudoers** is checked with `visudo -cf` before the file is installed, so a mistake cannot lock sudo out.
* **Passwordless sudo** means any program running as you gets root without a password. Use it only on a machine where you accept that.
* Keep a root terminal open the first time you try PAM changes. They have not been tried on a real reader or key yet.

markdown:
# Troubleshooting

Start with `bxrig status` and the doctors; each prints a fix next to every failed check.

|             Problem              |                Run                |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Something is missing after setup | `bxrig status`, then `bxrig init` |
| Installer failed                 | read `~/.cache/bxrig/install.log` |
| GPU or drivers                   | `bxrig gpu doctor`                |
| Magic Mouse, Trackpad, Bluetooth | `bxrig input doctor`              |
| Dolphin "Open with" is empty     | `bxrig dolphin doctor --fix`      |
| App launcher or menu             | `bxrig runner doctor`             |
| Containers                       | `bxrig containers doctor`         |
| Shortcuts clash                  | `bxrig keys conflicts`            |
| Plasma panels look wrong         | `bxrig plasma panels undo --yes`  |

## Exit codes

|  Code   |                         Meaning                         |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| 0       | done                                                    |
| 2       | a plan was printed (add `--yes`) or the usage was wrong |
| 4       | a precondition failed (a tool is missing, bad input)    |
| 5, 6, 7 | a step failed (7: some steps done, some failed)         |
| 9       | an internal error                                       |
| 10      | `update check`: an update is available                  |

Add `--json` to any command for machine-readable output.

markdown:
# Contributing and docs versions

BxRig is written in BoxLang and compiled with MatchBox. The code is in `src/`, tests in `tests/`, and every command is described in the [command contract](/architecture/COMMAND-CONTRACT/index.html).

## These docs

The docs are built with [bxSites](https://bxsites.io) from `docs/` and `bxsites.yaml` and published to GitHub Pages at <https://bxcachy.boxlang.io> by `.github/workflows/docs.yml` on every push to `development`.

```bash
bx-module install bx-sites
boxlang bxSites serve           # build and serve with live reload
boxlang bxSites build           # build to site/
```

## Versions

`docs/` is the version being written, **1.0.x**. When it ships:

```bash
boxlang bxSites version:new --name=1.0.x      # freeze a copy in docs/versions/1.0.x
```

Then set `versions.default: "1.0.x"` in `bxsites.yaml`: the release is served at the root and `docs/` becomes `/next/`. Every theme gets a version switcher. Patch releases edit `docs/versions/1.0.x/` in place; a new minor or major cuts a new version.

## Languages

English only for now. Add one with `boxlang bxSites i18n:new --code=es` and list it under `i18n.locales` in `bxsites.yaml`; `i18n:status` reports coverage.

## Releases

Pushes to `development` publish the `beta` channel; a `v*` tag publishes `stable`. See [Updates and channels](/guides/updates/index.html) and [Security](/guides/security/index.html).

markdown:
# Control Center

`bxrig tui` opens one terminal screen with a list of pages on the left and the open page on the right.

```bash
bxrig tui                   # opens on the Dashboard
bxrig tui --demo            # made-up data, nothing is run
bxrig tui dashboard --json  # the page's data, no terminal needed
```

## Icons

The page list and page headers carry Nerd Font icons when your terminal has the font (the BxRig wizard installs one for Starship). They are on when a Nerd Font is found, and you can force them: `bxrig tui --icons=on` or `--icons=off`, or set `BXRIG_ICONS`. Without the font they would show as boxes, so BxRig leaves them off. Emoji are not used, because terminals draw them two cells wide and the tables would not line up.

## Keys

|             Key              |                               What it does                                |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Tab, Shift+Tab (or `]`, `[`) | next and previous page                                                    |
| Left                         | move to the page list (Up and Down pick a page), Right or Enter goes back |
| q, Escape, Ctrl+c            | leave                                                                     |
| mouse                        | click a page or a row, scroll the wheel                                   |

The key bar at the bottom shows the keys of the page you are on.

## Dashboard

The first page shows what needs your attention, then the state of the machine:

* **Needs attention:** updates waiting, a backup older than two days (or none yet), a disk over 85% full, a battery under 20%. Move to a line and press Enter, or press its key, to see the plan of the fix. Nothing changes until you press `y`.
* **System:** CPU load, memory, disk and battery.
* **Running:** your databases and VMs, with ports.
* **Backups:** how fresh each place is. Enter opens BxTimeMachine, and you come back to the Dashboard when you leave it.

Each part is read on its own. If one cannot be read, the rest still shows.

## Pages

|   Page    |                                                                                          What it does                                                                                          |
|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dashboard | what needs attention, meters, what runs, backups                                                                                                                                               |
| BoxLang   | BoxLang versions through `bvm`: use, install, remove                                                                                                                                           |
| Java      | your Java homes: default, remove, and `a` to browse every JDK SDKMAN offers and install one (see `bxrig java`)                                                                                 |
| Maven     | every Maven version SDKMAN offers, installed ones marked: install, default, remove (see `bxrig sdk`)                                                                                           |
| Gradle    | the same for Gradle                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Versions  | BoxLang, MatchBox, Java and Node in one table; Enter opens the deep page                                                                                                                       |
| Ports     | what listens on which port and who owns it; stop or kill it, with a plan first. A port with two owners is red                                                                                  |
| Packages  | search the repos and the AUR with `/`, then install or remove                                                                                                                                  |
| Shortcuts | every shortcut; rebind (it asks for the keys), reset, conflicts                                                                                                                                |
| Machines  | your VMs (Windows and Linux desktops in containers): start, stop, info, new                                                                                                                    |
| Databases | the databases BxRig runs: start, stop, info, new                                                                                                                                               |
| Mail      | the mail your apps send to the catcher (`bxrig mail`): headers and text of the highlighted message, delete, clear, open it in the browser, send a test; it refreshes by itself every 3 seconds |
| Storage   | NAS shares and cloud remotes: mount, unmount, test                                                                                                                                             |
| Secrets   | names only; `v` shows one value for one look                                                                                                                                                   |
| Themes    | the 15 themes; Enter applies                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Logs      | the journal of this boot; `p` changes the lowest priority shown                                                                                                                                |

In a table, `/` filters the rows (or searches, on Packages), Enter keeps it and Escape clears it. Every key that changes something shows a plan first.

## How the pages fit together

Every screen shares one kit for lists, tabs, plan boxes and meters, so they look and behave the same. A page is a small class, which is also how new pages are added. A page can send you to a full screen such as BxTimeMachine and bring you back.

title: Mail catcher

# Mail catcher

When you build an app that sends email, you want to see the mail without sending it to anyone. `bxrig mail` runs a catcher in a container ([Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org)): your app sends to `127.0.0.1:1025` and the mail shows up in an inbox. Nothing leaves your machine.

```bash
bxrig mail start --yes        # plan first without --yes
bxrig mail env                # the settings to put in your app
bxrig mail test               # send one sample message
bxrig mail list               # what arrived
bxrig mail show ID            # headers, text body and attachments
bxrig mail open               # the web inbox in your browser
bxrig mail clear --yes        # delete every message
bxrig mail stop
```

The catcher listens on `127.0.0.1` only: SMTP on port 1025 (no TLS, any login is accepted) and the web inbox on port 8025. Change the ports with `--smtp-port=2525` and `--ui-port=9025`.

## Mail is thrown away when it stops

Without `--keep`, stopping the catcher deletes it and its mail. That is what you want while developing: every run starts with an empty inbox. If you want the mail to survive, start it with `bxrig mail start --keep --yes`; it is then stored in `~/.local/share/bxrig/mail`. `bxrig mail remove --yes` deletes the container and any stored mail (`--keep-data` keeps the folder).

## Settings for your app

`bxrig mail env` prints them for BoxLang and ColdBox apps, Laravel, Spring Boot, Node and plain environment variables. In short: host `127.0.0.1`, port `1025`, no encryption, no username or password.

## In the Control Center

`bxrig tui` has a Mail page. It lists the messages (newest first), shows the headers and text of the highlighted one, and refreshes itself every few seconds so you can watch mail arrive. `d` deletes a message, `c` clears the inbox, `o` opens it rendered in your browser and `t` sends a test message. Deleting and clearing show a plan first.

## In the wizard and the menu

The setup wizard has a yes or no question for the mail catcher (off by default). The task menu has Develop \> Mail catcher.

It needs a container engine: Podman by default, or Docker (`bxrig db engine docker`).
